revision.text:
The {{nihongo|'''Suwa clan'''|諏訪氏|Suwa-shi}} was a Japanese clan which claimed descent from the [[Seiwa Genji]]. It was a powerful clan of [[Shinano Province]], particularly during the [[Sengoku period]], when it had frequent clashes with its neighbor in Kai, the [[Takeda clan]]. The Suwa served as Takeda retainers for some time, and after the fall of the Takeda, reemerged. The family entered the [[Edo period]] as [[daimyo]], and eventually came to rule the [[Takashima Domain]] of [[Shinano Province]].
==References== * {{ja icon}} [http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html "Suwa-shi" on Harimaya.com] (1 March 2008) * {{ja icon}} [http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html "Takashima-han" on ''Edo 300 HTML''] (1 March 2008)
{{japan-hist-stub}}

{{Japanese name|Suwa}} {{Infobox Japanese clan |surname nihongo = 諏訪氏 |image = Image:Japanese crest Suwa Kajinoha(Black background).svg |image size = 140px |image caption = The emblem ([[Mon (badge)|''mon'']]) of the Suwa clan |home province =Suwa region (modern [[Chino, Nagano|Chino]], [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya]], [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa]] and [[Shimosuwa]]), [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] |parent house =Miwa/Jin clan or Kanasashi clan |titles =*Ōhori (Ōhafuri) of [[Suwa taisha]] *Daimyō |founder = [[Takeminakata]]<ref name="Picken">{{cite book|last1=Picken|first1=Stuart D.B.|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0810871724|page=288|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&pg=PA288}}</ref> or [[Seiwa Genji]] |final ruler = |current head = |founding year = |dissolution = |ruled until = |cadet branches = Takatoo clan }}
The {{nihongo|'''Suwa clan'''|諏訪氏|Suwa-shi}} was a Japanese clan hailing from the area encompassing [[Lake Suwa]] in [[Shinano Province]] (modern-day [[Nagano Prefecture]]). Originally a family of priests who served at the [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]]<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book|last1=Bocking|first1=Brian|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|date=2005|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1135797393|page=142|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6d-RAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA142}}</ref> and claimed descent from the shrine's deity, [[Takeminakata]] (also known as ''Suwa-myōjin''), by the [[Kamakura period]] the Suwa emerged and thrived as a prominent warrior clan with close ties to the [[Kamakura Shogunate|shogunate]].
Managing to survive the fall of both the Kamakura shogunate and the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which it supported), its feud with local rival clans, and frequent clashes with its neighbor in [[Kai Province|Kai]], the [[Takeda clan]], during the [[Sengoku period]], the clan split into two branches by the [[Edo period]]: one ruling the [[Suwa Domain]] of [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] as [[daimyō]], with the other continuing to serve as priests of Suwa Grand Shrine.
==Origins== The clan's actual origins are shrouded in mystery. Legend claims that the clan is descended from the [[Kami|god]] [[Takeminakata]], who, according to the ''[[Kojiki]]'', was driven to exile in Suwa after his defeat at the hands of [[Takemikazuchi]]. <ref name="Chamberlain">{{cite book|last1=Chamberlain|first1=Basil|title=A translation of the "Ko-ji-ki" or Records of Ancient Matters|date=1882|url=http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj039.htm#fn_697}}</ref><ref name="Hackin1932">{{cite book|author=J. Hackin|title=Asiatic Mythology: A Detailed Description and Explanation of the Mythologies of All the Great Nations of Asia|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HAZrFhvqnTkC&pg=PA395|year=1932|publisher=Asian Educational Services|isbn=978-81-206-0920-4|page=395}}</ref><ref name="Herbert2010">{{cite book|author=Jean Herbert|title=Shinto: At the Fountainhead of Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sg_JBQAAQBAJ&pg=PT437|date=18 October 2010|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90376-2|page=437}}</ref> According to lore passed down in the Suwa region, Takeminakata, upon his arrival at Suwa, defeated Moreya (洩矢神 ''Moreya-no-kami''), a local god who originally ruled Suwa and who tried to prevent Takeminakata from entering his land.
Upon his victory over Moreya, Takeminakata then became the new god of Suwa,<ref name="呉清恵2011">{{cite book|author=呉清恵|title=Cosmogonical Worldview of Jomon Pottery|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hxulspIN_2UC&pg=PA157|date=November 2011|publisher=株式会社 三恵社|isbn=978-4-88361-924-5|page=157}}</ref><ref name="Ashkenazi2003">{{cite book|author=Michael Ashkenazi|title=Handbook of Japanese Mythology|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gqs-y9R2AekC&pg=PA267|date=1 January 2003|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-57607-467-1|pages=267–268}}</ref> enshrined with his consort Yasakatome in Suwa Grand Shrine (''Suwa-taisha''), a complex of four shrines grouped into two sites: the Upper Shrine or ''Kamisha'' (上社) located south of [[Lake Suwa]], and the Lower Shrine or ''Shimosha'' (下社) on the northern side of the lake. Both Moreya and Takeminakata are said to have subsequently become the ancestors of two locally-prominent clans which served as priests of the ''Kamisha'', the Moriya (守矢氏) and the Suwa clans, respectively.<ref name="Picken" /> <ref name ="Jinchokan">{{cite web|title=Brochure of the Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (神長官守矢資料館のしおり)|url=http://www.komainu.org/nagano/chinosi/MishagujiSousha/siori.pdf}} {{ja icon}}</ref>
Other claimed ancestors of the clan include the [[Emperor Kanmu]] - who was said to have had a son named Arigasu (有員親王 ''Arigasu-shinnō''), to whom the god of Suwa [[Spirit possession|descended]] and conferred the priesthood<ref>{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=}}</ref> - or the [[Seiwa Genji]] (to which many warrior clans claimed descent from).<ref name="Harimaya">{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}}</ref> <ref name="Papinot">{{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=611|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}}</ref> ==History==
In antiquity, one member of the clan's main family served as ''ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''ōhafuri'') of the ''Kamisha'', considered to be the visible embodiment of the god of Suwa himself and as such, [[Arahitogami|a living deity]] and an object of worship in his own right. <ref>{{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}}</ref> The ''ōhōri'' in turn was assisted by five priests headed by the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), a position occupied by the Moriya clan. The ''jinchōkan'' was responsible for overseeing the ''Kamisha'' 's rituals in general as well as summoning [[Mishaguji]] (a god or gods worshipped in Suwa since ancient times) to possess the ''ōhōri'' during certain occasions, such as his investiture into the office.<ref>{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}}</ref>
In the meantime, members of the clan who did not serve as priests began to take up arms and pursue military careers. By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]].
During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan (金刺氏),<ref>{{cite web|title=金刺氏|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/kanazasi.html|website=harimaya.com}}</ref> which held the position of ''ōhori'' of the Lower Shrine (''Shimosha'') and which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties formerly held by the main house. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601.<ref name="Harimaya" /> <ref name="Papinot" />
Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方''').
All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].<ref>{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML}} {{ja icon}}</ref>
Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control.
The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', Hiroshi (諏方弘), the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.<ref>{{cite web|title=最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} {{ja icon}}</ref>
==References== {{Reflist|30em}}

Legend claims that the clan is descended from the [[Kami|god]] [[Takeminakata]], who, according to the ''[[Kojiki]]'', was driven to exile in Suwa after his defeat at the hands of [[Takemikazuchi]]. <ref name="Chamberlain">{{cite book|last1=Chamberlain|first1=Basil|title=A translation of the "Ko-ji-ki" or Records of Ancient Matters|date=1882|url=http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj039.htm#fn_697}}</ref><ref name="Hackin1932">{{cite book|author=J. Hackin|title=Asiatic Mythology: A Detailed Description and Explanation of the Mythologies of All the Great Nations of Asia|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HAZrFhvqnTkC&pg=PA395|year=1932|publisher=Asian Educational Services|isbn=978-81-206-0920-4|page=395}}</ref><ref name="Herbert2010">{{cite book|author=Jean Herbert|title=Shinto: At the Fountainhead of Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sg_JBQAAQBAJ&pg=PT437|date=18 October 2010|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90376-2|page=437}}</ref> According to lore passed down in the Suwa region, Takeminakata, upon his arrival at Suwa, defeated Moreya (洩矢神 ''Moreya-no-kami''), a local god who originally ruled Suwa and who tried to prevent Takeminakata from entering his land.
Upon his victory over Moreya, Takeminakata then became the new god of Suwa,<ref name="呉清恵2011">{{cite book|author=呉清恵|title=Cosmogonical Worldview of Jomon Pottery|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hxulspIN_2UC&pg=PA157|date=November 2011|publisher=株式会社 三恵社|isbn=978-4-88361-924-5|page=157}}</ref><ref name="Ashkenazi2003">{{cite book|author=Michael Ashkenazi|title=Handbook of Japanese Mythology|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gqs-y9R2AekC&pg=PA267|date=1 January 2003|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-57607-467-1|pages=267–268}}</ref> enshrined with his consort Yasakatome in Suwa Grand Shrine (''Suwa-taisha''), a complex of four shrines grouped into two sites: the Upper Shrine or ''Kamisha'' (上社) located south of [[Lake Suwa]], and the Lower Shrine or ''Shimosha'' (下社) on the northern side of the lake. Both Moreya and Takeminakata are said to have subsequently become the ancestors of two locally-prominent clans which served as priests of the ''Kamisha'', the Moriya (守矢氏) and the Suwa clans, respectively.<ref name="Picken" /> <ref name ="Jinchokan">{{cite web|title=Brochure of the Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (神長官守矢資料館のしおり)|url=http://www.komainu.org/nagano/chinosi/MishagujiSousha/siori.pdf}} {{ja icon}}</ref>
Other claimed ancestors of the clan include the [[Emperor Kanmu]] - who was said to have had a son named Arigasu (有員親王 ''Arigasu-shinnō''), to whom the god of Suwa [[Spirit possession|descended]] and conferred the priesthood<ref>{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=}}</ref> - or the [[Seiwa Genji]] (to which many warrior clans claimed descent from).<ref name="Harimaya">{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}}</ref> <ref name="Papinot">{{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=611|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}}</ref> ==History==
In antiquity, one member of the clan's main family served as ''ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''ōhafuri'') of the ''Kamisha'', considered to be the visible embodiment of the god of Suwa himself and as such, [[Arahitogami|a living deity]] and an object of worship in his own right. <ref>{{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}}</ref> The ''ōhōri'' in turn was assisted by five priests headed by the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), a position occupied by the Moriya clan. The ''jinchōkan'' was responsible for overseeing the ''Kamisha'' 's rituals in general as well as summoning [[Mishaguji]] (a god or gods worshipped in Suwa since ancient times) to possess the ''ōhōri'' during certain occasions, such as his investiture into the office.<ref>{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}}</ref>
In the meantime, members of the clan who did not serve as priests began to take up arms and pursue military careers. By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]].
During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan (金刺氏),<ref>{{cite web|title=金刺氏|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/kanazasi.html|website=harimaya.com}}</ref> which held the position of ''ōhori'' of the Lower Shrine (''Shimosha'') and which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties formerly held by the main house. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601.<ref name="Harimaya" /> <ref name="Papinot" />
[[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the Moriya clan's estate grounds in [[Chino, Nagano|Chino City]], Nagano.]]Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方''').
All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].<ref>{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML}} {{ja icon}}</ref>
Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control.
The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', Hiroshi (諏方弘), the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.<ref>{{cite web|title=最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} {{ja icon}}</ref>

Both Moreya and Takeminakata are said to have subsequently become the ancestors of two locally-prominent clans which served as priests of the ''Kamisha'', the Moriya (守矢氏) and the Suwa clans, respectively. {{cite web|title=Brochure of the Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (神長官守矢資料館のしおり)|url=http://www.komainu.org/nagano/chinosi/MishagujiSousha/siori.pdf}} {{ja icon}} Other claimed ancestors of the clan include the [[Emperor Kanmu]] - who was said to have had a son named Arigasu (有員親王 ''Arigasu-shinnō''), to whom the god of Suwa [[Spirit possession|descended]] and conferred the priesthood{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=}} - or the [[Seiwa Genji]] (to which many warrior clans claimed descent from).{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}} {{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=611|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}} ==History== In antiquity, one member of the clan's main family served as ''ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''ōhafuri'') of the ''Kamisha'', considered to be the visible embodiment of the god of Suwa himself and as such, [[Arahitogami|a living deity]] and an object of worship in his own right. {{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}}{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}} The ''ōhōri'' in turn was assisted by five priests headed by the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), a position occupied by the Moriya clan. The ''jinchōkan'' was responsible for overseeing the ''Kamisha'' 's rituals in general as well as summoning [[Mishaguji]] (a god or gods worshipped in Suwa since ancient times) to possess the ''ōhōri'' during certain occasions, such as his investiture into the office.{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} In the meantime, members of the clan who did not serve as priests began to take up arms and pursue military careers. By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]]. During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan (金刺氏),{{cite web|title=金刺氏|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/kanazasi.html|website=harimaya.com}} which held the position of ''ōhori'' of the Lower Shrine (''Shimosha'') and which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties formerly held by the main house. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601. [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the Moriya clan's estate grounds in [[Chino, Nagano|Chino City]], Nagano.]]Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方'''). All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML}} {{ja icon}} Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control. The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', Hiroshi (諏方弘), the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.{{cite web|title=最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} {{ja icon}} ==See also== *[[Takeminakata]] *[[Suwa Domain]] *[[Suwa taisha]] *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Takeda Shingen]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} {{Japan-clan-stub}} [[Category:Japanese clans]]

Both Moreya and Takeminakata are said to have subsequently become the ancestors of two locally-prominent clans which served as priests of the ''Kamisha'', the Moriya (守矢氏) and the Suwa clans, respectively. {{cite web|title=Brochure of the Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (神長官守矢資料館のしおり)|url=http://www.komainu.org/nagano/chinosi/MishagujiSousha/siori.pdf}} {{ja icon}} Other claimed ancestors of the clan include the [[Emperor Kanmu]] - who was said to have had a son named Arigasu (有員親王 ''Arigasu-shinnō''), to whom the god of Suwa [[Spirit possession|descended]] and conferred the priesthood{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=}} - or the [[Seiwa Genji]] (to which many warrior clans claimed descent from).{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}} {{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=611|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}} ==History== In antiquity, one member of the clan's main family served as ''ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''ōhafuri'') of the ''Kamisha'', considered to be the visible embodiment of the god of Suwa himself and as such, [[Arahitogami|a living deity]] and an object of worship in his own right. {{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}}{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}} The ''ōhōri'' in turn was assisted by five priests headed by the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), a position occupied by the Moriya clan. The ''jinchōkan'' was responsible for overseeing the ''Kamisha'' 's rituals in general as well as summoning [[Mishaguji]] (a god or gods worshipped in Suwa since ancient times) to possess the ''ōhōri'' during certain occasions, such as his investiture into the office.{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} In the meantime, members of the clan who did not serve as priests began to take up arms and pursue military careers. By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]]. During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan (金刺氏),{{cite web|title=金刺氏|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/kanazasi.html|website=harimaya.com}} which held the position of ''ōhori'' of the Lower Shrine (''Shimosha'') and which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties formerly held by the main house. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601. [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the Moriya clan's estate grounds in [[Chino, Nagano|Chino City]], Nagano.]]Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方'''). All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML}} {{ja icon}} Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control. The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', Hiroshi (諏方弘), the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.{{cite web|title=最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} {{ja icon}} ==See also== *[[Takeminakata]] *[[Suwa Domain]] *[[Suwa taisha]] *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Takeda Shingen]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} {{Japan-clan-stub}} [[Category:Japanese clans]]

Both Moreya and Takeminakata are said to have subsequently become the ancestors of two locally-prominent clans which served as priests of the ''Kamisha'', the Moriya (守矢氏) and the Suwa clans, respectively. {{cite web|title=Brochure of the Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (神長官守矢資料館のしおり)|url=http://www.komainu.org/nagano/chinosi/MishagujiSousha/siori.pdf}} {{ja icon}} Other claimed ancestors of the clan include the [[Emperor Kanmu]] - via a supposed son, Prince Arigasu (有員親王 ''Arigasu-shinnō''), upon whom the god of Suwa [[Spirit possession|descended]]{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=}} - or the [[Seiwa Genji]] (to which many warrior clans claimed descent from).{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}} {{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=611|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}} ==History== In antiquity, one member of the clan's main family served as ''ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''ōhafuri'') of the ''Kamisha'', considered to be the visible embodiment of the god of Suwa himself and as such, [[Arahitogami|a living deity]] and an object of worship in his own right. {{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}}{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}} The ''ōhōri'' in turn was assisted by five priests headed by the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), a position occupied by the Moriya clan. The ''jinchōkan'' was responsible for overseeing the ''Kamisha'' 's rituals in general as well as summoning [[Mishaguji]] (a god or gods worshipped in Suwa since ancient times) to possess the ''ōhōri'' during certain occasions, such as his investiture into the office.{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} In the meantime, members of the clan who did not serve as priests began to take up arms and pursue military careers. By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]]. During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan (金刺氏),{{cite web|title=金刺氏|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/kanazasi.html|website=harimaya.com}} which held the position of ''ōhori'' of the Lower Shrine (''Shimosha'') and which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties formerly held by the main house. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601. [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the Moriya clan's estate grounds in [[Chino, Nagano|Chino City]], Nagano.]]Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方'''). All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML}} {{ja icon}} Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control. The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', Hiroshi (諏方弘), the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.{{cite web|title=最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} {{ja icon}} ==See also== *[[Takeminakata]] *[[Suwa Domain]] *[[Suwa taisha]] *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Takeda Shingen]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} {{Japan-clan-stub}} [[Category:Japanese clans]]

Both Moreya and Takeminakata are said to have subsequently become the ancestors of two locally-prominent clans which served as priests of the ''Kamisha'', the Moriya (守矢氏) and the Suwa clans, respectively. {{cite web|title=Brochure of the Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (神長官守矢資料館のしおり)|url=http://www.komainu.org/nagano/chinosi/MishagujiSousha/siori.pdf}} {{ja icon}} Other claimed ancestors of the clan include the [[Emperor Kanmu]] - via a supposed son, Prince Arigasu (有員親王 ''Arigasu-shinnō''), upon whom the god of Suwa [[Spirit possession|descended]]{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=}} - or the [[Seiwa Genji]] (to which many warrior clans claimed descent from).{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}} {{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=611|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}} ==History== In antiquity, one member of the clan served as ''ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''ōhafuri'') of the ''Kamisha'', considered to be the visible embodiment of the god of Suwa himself and as such, [[Arahitogami|a living deity]] and an object of worship in his own right. {{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}}{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}} The ''ōhōri'' was assisted by five priests headed by the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), a position occupied by the Moriya clan. The ''jinchōkan'' was responsible for overseeing the ''Kamisha'''s rituals in general as well as summoning [[Mishaguji]] (a god or gods worshipped in Suwa since ancient times) to possess the ''ōhōri'' during certain occasions, such as his investiture into the office.{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} In the meantime, members of the clan who did not serve as priests began to take up arms and pursue military careers. By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]]. During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan (金刺氏),{{cite web|title=金刺氏|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/kanazasi.html|website=harimaya.com}} which held the position of ''ōhori'' of the Lower Shrine (''Shimosha'') and which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties formerly held by the main house. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601. [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the Moriya clan's estate grounds in [[Chino, Nagano|Chino City]], Nagano.]]Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方'''). All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML}} {{ja icon}} Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control. The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', Hiroshi (諏方弘), the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.{{cite web|title=最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} {{ja icon}} ==See also== *[[Takeminakata]] *[[Suwa Domain]] *[[Suwa taisha]] *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Takeda Shingen]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} {{Japan-clan-stub}} [[Category:Japanese clans]]

Both Moreya and Takeminakata are said to have subsequently become the ancestors of two locally-prominent clans which served as priests of the ''Kamisha'', the Moriya (守矢氏) and the Suwa clans, respectively. {{cite web|title=Brochure of the Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (神長官守矢資料館のしおり)|url=http://www.komainu.org/nagano/chinosi/MishagujiSousha/siori.pdf}} {{ja icon}} Other claimed ancestors of the clan include the [[Emperor Kanmu]] - via a supposed son, Prince Arigasu (有員親王 ''Arigasu-shinnō''), upon whom the god of Suwa [[Spirit possession|descended]]{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=}} - or the [[Seiwa Genji]] (to which many warrior clans claimed descent from).{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}} {{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=611|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}} ==History== In antiquity, one member of the clan served as ''ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''ōhafuri'') of the ''Kamisha'', considered to be the visible embodiment of the god of Suwa himself and as such, [[Arahitogami|a living deity]] and an object of worship in his own right. {{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}}{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}} The ''ōhōri'' was assisted by five priests headed by the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), a position occupied by the Moriya clan. The ''jinchōkan'' was responsible for overseeing the ''Kamisha'''s rituals in general as well as summoning [[Mishaguji]] (a god or gods worshipped in Suwa since ancient times, which it was believed only the Moriya could call upon) to possess the ''ōhōri'' during certain occasions, such as his investiture into the office.{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} Though officially the chief priest of the upper shrine and a living god, the ''ōhōri'' had little, if any, actual power, which rested in the hands of the Moriya ''jinchōkan''. It was even forbidden for the ''ōhōri'' to step foot outside Suwa; breaking this ban was thought to incur the wrath of Mishaguji. In the meantime, members of the clan who did not serve as priests began to take up arms and pursue military careers. By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]]. During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan (金刺氏),{{cite web|title=金刺氏|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/kanazasi.html|website=harimaya.com}} which held the position of ''ōhori'' of the Lower Shrine (''Shimosha'') and which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties formerly held by the main house. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601. [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the Moriya clan's estate grounds in [[Chino, Nagano|Chino City]], Nagano.]]Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方'''). All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML}} {{ja icon}} Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control. The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', Hiroshi (諏方弘), the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.{{cite web|title=最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} {{ja icon}} ==See also== *[[Takeminakata]] *[[Suwa Domain]] *[[Suwa taisha]] *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Takeda Shingen]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} {{Japan-clan-stub}} [[Category:Japanese clans]]

Both Moreya and Takeminakata are said to have subsequently become the ancestors of two locally-prominent clans which served as priests of the ''Kamisha'', the Moriya (守矢氏) and the Suwa clans, respectively. {{cite web|title=Brochure of the Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (神長官守矢資料館のしおり)|url=http://www.komainu.org/nagano/chinosi/MishagujiSousha/siori.pdf}} {{ja icon}} Other claimed ancestors of the clan include the [[Emperor Kanmu]] - via a supposed son, Prince Arigasu (有員親王 ''Arigasu-shinnō''), upon whom the god of Suwa [[Spirit possession|descended]]{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=}} - or the [[Seiwa Genji]] (to which many warrior clans claimed descent from).{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}} {{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=611|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}} ==History== ===Ōhōri=== In antiquity, one member of the clan served as ''ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''ōhafuri'') of the ''Kamisha'', considered to be the visible embodiment of the god of Suwa himself and as such, [[Arahitogami|a living god]] (''arahitogami'') and an object of worship in his own right. {{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}}{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}} The ''ōhōri'', who traditionally assumed the position at the young age of eight, was assisted by five priests headed by the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), a position occupied by the Moriya clan. The ''jinchōkan'' was responsible for overseeing the ''Kamisha'''s rites and ceremonies in general, as well as summoning [[Mishaguji]] (a god or gods worshipped in Suwa since ancient times who is/are sometimes conflated with Takeminakata/Suwa-myōjin) to possess the ''ōhōri'' during certain occasions, such as his investiture into the office.{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} Though officially the chief priest of the upper shrine and a living deity, the Suwa ''ōhōri'' had little, if any, actual power, which rested in the hands of the Moriya ''jinchōkan'', who was the only one believed to be able to summon the gods. It was even forbidden for the ''ōhōri'' to ever leave Suwa; breaking this ban was thought to incur the wrath of Mishaguji.{{cite web|title=諏訪大明神 (Suwa-daimyōjin)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E5%A4%A7%E6%98%8E%E7%A5%9E.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} ===From the Kamakura period to the Sengoku period=== In the meantime, members of the clan who did not serve as priests began to take up arms and pursue military careers. By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]]. During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan (金刺氏),{{cite web|title=金刺氏|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/kanazasi.html|website=harimaya.com}} which held the position of ''ōhori'' of the Lower Shrine (''Shimosha'') and which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties formerly held by the main house. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601. ===Edo period onwards=== [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the Moriya clan's estate grounds in [[Chino, Nagano|Chino City]], Nagano.]]Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方'''). All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML}} {{ja icon}} Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control. The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', Hiroshi (諏方弘), the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.{{cite web|title=最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} {{ja icon}} ==See also== *[[Takeminakata]] *[[Suwa Domain]] *[[Suwa taisha]] *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Takeda Shingen]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} {{Japan-clan-stub}} [[Category:Japanese clans]]

{{Japanese name|Suwa}} {{Infobox Japanese clan |surname nihongo = 諏訪氏 |image = Image:Japanese crest Suwa Kajinoha(Black background).svg |image size = 140px |image caption = The emblem ([[Mon (badge)|''mon'']]) of the Suwa clan |home province =Suwa region (modern [[Chino, Nagano|Chino]], [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya]], [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa]] and [[Shimosuwa]]), [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] |parent house =Kanasashi clan? |titles =*''Ōhōri'' (''Ōhafuri'') of [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]] *Daimyō |founder = Unknown; see 'Ancestry' |final ruler = |current head = |founding year = |dissolution = |ruled until = |cadet branches = Suwa clan (諏方氏) (defunct)
Takatoo clan (高遠氏)
Hoshina clan (保科氏)
Chino clan (千野氏) }} The {{nihongo|'''Suwa clan'''|諏訪氏|Suwa-shi}} was a Japanese clan hailing from the area encompassing [[Lake Suwa]] in [[Shinano Province]] (modern-day [[Nagano Prefecture]]). Originally a family of priests who served at the [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]]{{cite book|last1=Bocking|first1=Brian|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|date=2005|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1135797393|page=142|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6d-RAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA142}}, by the [[Kamakura period]] the clan - now named 'Suwa' - thrived as a prominent warrior clan with close ties to the [[Kamakura Shogunate|shogunate]]. Managing to survive the fall of both the Kamakura shogunate and the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] which it supported, its feud with local rival clans, and frequent clashes with its neighbor in [[Kai Province|Kai]], the [[Takeda clan]], during the [[Sengoku period]] (which ended in the extinction of the main family), the clan split into two branches by the [[Edo period]]: one ruling the [[Suwa Domain]] of [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] as [[daimyō]], with the other continuing to serve as priests of Suwa Grand Shrine. ==Ancestry== The clan's actual ancestry is shrouded in mystery. Legend claims that the clan is descended from the [[Kami|god]] [[Takeminakata]] (also known as ''Suwa-myōjin''), who in the ''[[Kojiki]]'' was driven to exile in Suwa after his defeat at the hands of [[Takemikazuchi]]. {{cite book|last1=Chamberlain|first1=Basil|title=A translation of the "Ko-ji-ki" or Records of Ancient Matters|date=1882|url=http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj039.htm#fn_697}}{{cite book|author=J. Hackin|title=Asiatic Mythology: A Detailed Description and Explanation of the Mythologies of All the Great Nations of Asia|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HAZrFhvqnTkC&pg=PA395|year=1932|publisher=Asian Educational Services|isbn=978-81-206-0920-4|page=395}}{{cite book|author=Jean Herbert|title=Shinto: At the Fountainhead of Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sg_JBQAAQBAJ&pg=PT437|date=18 October 2010|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90376-2|page=437}} According to lore passed down in the Suwa region, Takeminakata, upon his arrival at Suwa, fought against Moreya (洩矢神 ''Moreya-no-kami''), a local deity who tried to prevent Takeminakata from entering his domain. Upon the defeat and submission of Moreya and the other indigenous gods of the region, Takeminakata then became the new god of Suwa,{{cite book|author=呉清恵|title=Cosmogonical Worldview of Jomon Pottery|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hxulspIN_2UC&pg=PA157|date=November 2011|publisher=株式会社　三恵社|isbn=978-4-88361-924-5|page=157}}{{cite book|author=Michael Ashkenazi|title=Handbook of Japanese Mythology|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gqs-y9R2AekC&pg=PA267|date=1 January 2003|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-57607-467-1|pages=267–268}} enshrined with his consort Yasakatome in [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]], a complex of four shrines grouped into two sites: the Upper Shrine or ''Kamisha'' (上社) located south of [[Lake Suwa]], and the Lower Shrine or ''Shimosha'' (下社) on the northern side of the lake. Both Moreya and Takeminakata are said to have subsequently become the ancestors of two locally-prominent clans which served as priests of the ''Kamisha'', the Moriya (守矢氏) and the Suwa clans, respectively.{{cite book|last1=Picken|first1=Stuart D.B.|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0810871724|page=288|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&pg=PA288}} {{cite web|title=Brochure of the Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (神長官守矢資料館のしおり)|url=http://www.komainu.org/nagano/chinosi/MishagujiSousha/siori.pdf}} {{ja icon}} Other claimed ancestors of the clan include the [[Emperor Kanmu]] - via a supposed son, Prince Arikazu (有員親王 ''Arikazu-shinnō''), upon whom the god of Suwa [[Spirit possession|came down]] (see 'As ''ōhōri''' section below) - or the [[Seiwa Genji]] (to which many warrior clans claimed descent from).{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}} {{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=611|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}} It has also been suggested that the Suwa and the Kanasashi clans (金刺氏), which served as ''ōhōri'' of the ''Shimosha'' and claimed descendants of the [[Kuni no miyatsuko|kuni-no-miyatsuko]] of [[Shinano Province]] (the [[Yamato period|Yamato court]]'s representative in the region), were originally one and the same clan, noting while the name 'Kanasashi' is already attested in sources from the [[Nara period|Nara]] and [[Heian period|Heian]] periods, the names 'Suwa' and 'Miwa' (神, also read as 'Shin' or 'Jin') do not appear in written records until the Kamakura period, around the same time the sources begin to distinguish clearly between the Suwa ''Kamisha'' and the ''Shimosha'' (earlier records still treat the shrines at Suwa as a single entity).{{cite web|title=金刺氏 (Kanasashi-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/kanazasi.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}} ==History== ===As ''ōhōri''=== In antiquity, one member of the clan served as ''ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''ōhafuri'') of the ''Kamisha'', considered to be the visible embodiment of Suwa-myōjin himself and as such, [[Arahitogami|a living god]] (''arahitogami'') and an object of worship in his own right. {{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}} {{ja icon}}{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}} The ''ōhōri'', who traditionally assumed the position at a young age, was assisted by five priests ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=u2Mf7Ef60FkC&pg=PA11 諏訪史年表] (Suwa Shinenpyō).'' Nagano: Suwa Kyōikukai. p. 11. {{ja icon}}神氏系図 (''Miwa-shi keizu'') in Miyachi, Naokazu (1931). [http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1076393/166 諏訪史 (Suwa-shi), vol. 2]. 信濃教育会諏訪部会 (Shinano kyōikukai Suwa-bukai). - saw the god of Suwa at age of eight. The god, declaring that since he has no visible body his priest (''hōri'') shall be considered his living incarnation, took off his robe and made the boy wear it, thus conferring both priesthood and divinity to him. Since then, Otoei (or Arikazu) and their descendants became known as ''misogi-no-hōri'' (御衣着祝), the precursor to the title of ''ōhōri''. ===From the Kamakura period to the Sengoku period=== In the meantime, members of the clan who did not serve as priests apparently began to take up arms and pursue military careers. With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方'''). All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML}} {{ja icon}} Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine.
