{{Japanese name|Suwa}} {{Infobox Japanese clan |surname nihongo = 諏訪氏 |image = Image:Japanese crest Suwa Kajinoha(Black background).svg |image size = 140px |image caption = The emblem ([[Mon (badge)|''mon'']]) of the Suwa clan |home province =Suwa region (modern [[Chino, Nagano|Chino]], [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya]], [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa]] and [[Shimosuwa]]), [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] |parent house =Kanasashi clan? |titles =*''Ōhōri'' (''Ōhafuri'') of [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]] *Daimyō |founder = Unknown; see 'Ancestry' |final ruler = |current head = |founding year = |dissolution = |ruled until = |cadet branches = Suwa clan (諏方氏) (defunct)
Takatoo clan (高遠氏)
Hoshina clan (保科氏)
Chino clan (千野氏) }} The {{nihongo|'''Suwa clan'''|諏訪氏|Suwa-shi}} was a Japanese clan hailing from the area encompassing [[Lake Suwa]] in [[Shinano Province]] (modern-day [[Nagano Prefecture]]). Originally a family of priests who served at the [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]],{{cite book|last1=Bocking|first1=Brian|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|date=2005|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1135797393|page=142|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6d-RAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA142}} by the [[Kamakura period]] the clan - now named 'Suwa' - thrived as a prominent warrior clan with close ties to the [[Kamakura Shogunate|shogunate]]. Managing to survive the fall of both the Kamakura shogunate and the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] which it supported, its feud with local rival clans, and frequent clashes with its neighbor in [[Kai Province|Kai]], the [[Takeda clan]], during the [[Sengoku period]] (which ended in the extinction of the main family), the clan split into two branches by the [[Edo period]]: one ruling the [[Suwa Domain]] of [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] as [[daimyō]], with the other continuing to serve as priests of Suwa Grand Shrine. ==Ancestry== The clan's actual origins are shrouded in mystery. Legend claims that the clan is descended from the [[Kami|god]] of [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]], Suwa-myōjin, most often identified with [[Takeminakata]] of the ''[[Kojiki]]'', who was driven to exile in Suwa after his defeat at the hands of [[Takemikazuchi]], a messenger sent by the gods of [[Takama-ga-hara|heaven]] to claim the land held by his father [[Ōkuninushi]] in the name of the goddess [[Amaterasu]].{{cite book|last1=Chamberlain|first1=Basil|title=A translation of the "Ko-ji-ki" or Records of Ancient Matters|date=1882|url=http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj039.htm#fn_697}}{{cite book|author=J. Hackin|title=Asiatic Mythology: A Detailed Description and Explanation of the Mythologies of All the Great Nations of Asia|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HAZrFhvqnTkC&pg=PA395|year=1932|publisher=Asian Educational Services|isbn=978-81-206-0920-4|page=395}}{{cite book|author=Jean Herbert|title=Shinto: At the Fountainhead of Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sg_JBQAAQBAJ&pg=PT437|date=18 October 2010|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90376-2|page=437}} According to local tradition, Suwa-myōjin, a god who came from outside Suwa, fought against local gods who resisted his entry into the region such as [[Moreya]]. Upon their defeat and submission, Suwa-myōjin/Takeminakata then became the new chief god of Suwa,{{cite book|author=呉清恵|title=Cosmogonical Worldview of Jomon Pottery|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hxulspIN_2UC&pg=PA157|date=November 2011|publisher=株式会社　三恵社|isbn=978-4-88361-924-5|page=157}}{{cite book|author=Michael Ashkenazi|title=Handbook of Japanese Mythology|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gqs-y9R2AekC&pg=PA267|date=1 January 2003|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-57607-467-1|pages=267–268}} enshrined with his consort Yasakatome in Suwa Grand Shrine, a complex of four shrines grouped into two sites: the Upper Shrine or ''Kamisha'' (上社) located south of [[Lake Suwa]], and the Lower Shrine or ''Shimosha'' (下社) on the northern side of the lake. Both Moreya and Suwa-myōjin are said to have subsequently become the ancestors of two locally-prominent clans which served as priests of the ''Kamisha'', the Moriya (守矢氏) and the Suwa clans, respectively.{{cite book|last1=Picken|first1=Stuart D.B.|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0810871724|page=288|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&pg=PA288}}{{cite web|title=Brochure of the Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (神長官守矢資料館のしおり)|url=http://www.komainu.org/nagano/chinosi/MishagujiSousha/siori.pdf}} {{ja icon}} Other claimed ancestors of the clan include the [[Emperor Kanmu]] - via a supposed son named Arikazu (see 'As ''ōhōri''' section below) - or the [[Seiwa Genji]] via Minamoto no Mitsuyasu (one of the sons of [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto]]).{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}}{{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=611|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}} It has also been theorized that historically, the Suwa may have actually originated from the Kanasashi clan (金刺氏), which in turn branched out from the clan of the provincial governors or ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko|kuni-no-miyatsuko]]'' of [[Shinano Province]] (the [[Yamato period|Yamato court]]'s representatives in the region) and were the chief priests or ''ōhōri'' of the ''Shimosha'', noting while the name 'Kanasashi' is already attested in sources from the [[Nara period|Nara]] and [[Heian period|Heian]] periods, the names 'Suwa' and 'Miwa' (神, also read as 'Shin' or 'Jin') do not appear in written records until the Kamakura period, around the same time sources begin to distinguish between the Suwa ''Kamisha'' and the ''Shimosha'' (earlier records still treat the shrines at Suwa more or less as a single entity).{{cite web|title=金刺氏 (Kanasashi-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/kanazasi.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}} Seemingly supporting this theory is the genealogical record of the Aso clan ([[:ja:阿蘇氏|阿蘇氏]]) of [[Aso Shrine]] (said to be related to the Kanasashi), which list both the Kanasashi and the Suwa as being of the same lineage.{{cite book|author=Rekishi REAL Henshūbu (歴史REAL編集部) (ed.)|title=Jinja to kodai gōzoku no nazo (神社と古代豪族の謎)|date=2016|publisher=Yosensha|isbn=978-4800308924|page=40}} {{ja icon}}{{cite book|last1=Miyasaka|first1=Mitsuaki|title=諏訪大社の御柱と年中行事 (Suwa-taisha no Onbashira to nenchu-gyōji)|date=1992|publisher=Kyōdo shuppansha|isbn=978-4876631780|pages=7}} {{ja icon}} ==History== ===As ''ōhōri''=== In antiquity, one member of the clan served as ''ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''ōhafuri'') of the ''Kamisha'', considered to be the visible embodiment of Suwa-myōjin himself and as such, [[Arahitogami|a living god]] (''arahitogami'') and an object of worship in his own right.{{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}} {{ja icon}}{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}} The ''ōhōri'', who traditionally assumed the position at a young age, was assisted by five priests headed by the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), a position occupied by the Moriya clan. Among the ''jinchōkan'''s roles were overseeing the ''Kamisha'''s rites and ceremonies in general, as well as summoning [[Mishaguji]] (a god or gods worshipped in Suwa since ancient times who is/are sometimes conflated with Takeminakata/Suwa-myōjin) to possess chosen individuals or inhabit inanimate objects during ceremonies when the presence of the god was called for.Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya-jinchō-ke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 4. {{ja icon}}Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In {{cite book|author1=Ueda|author2=Gorai|author3=Ōbayashi|author4=Miyasaka, M.|author5=Miyasaka, Y.|title=御柱祭と諏訪大社 (Onbashira-sai to Suwa-taisha)|location=Nagano|publisher=Chikuma Shobō|isbn=978-4480841810|pages=25-26}} {{ja icon}} According to legend, the very first priest - a boy by the age of eight - was chosen by Suwa-myōjin himself in a vision. The god, declaring that since he (the god) has no tangible physical form his priest (''hōri'') shall be worshipped instead as his embodiment, took off his robe and made the boy wear it, thus conferring both priesthood and divinity to him. Since then, the boy and his descendants who assumed the same office became known as ''misogi-no-hōri'' (御衣着祝 'priest (who) wears the sacred garment'), the precursor to the title of ''ōhōri''. The boy in the story has variously been identified with two semi-legendary individuals: Otoei (乙頴, also 'Otsuei'), also known as Kumako (神子 or 熊子), who supposedly lived around the time of [[Emperor Yōmei]] (585-587){{cite book|last1=Iida|first1=Kōtarō|title=諏訪史料 (Suwa shiryō), vol. 1|date=1898|page=5|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/765163/9}}Miyasaka (1992), pp. 7–11., and Arikazu (有員), claimed to have lived during the reign of [[Emperor Kanmu]] around the 9th century and sometimes even portrayed as the latter's son.{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=|page=8}}Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=u2Mf7Ef60FkC&pg=PA11 諏訪史年表] (Suwa Shinenpyō).'' Nagano: Suwa Kyōikukai. p. 11. {{ja icon}}神氏系図 (''Miwa-shi keizu'') in Miyachi, Naokazu (1931). [http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1076393/166 諏訪史 (Suwa-shi), vol. 2]. 信濃教育会諏訪部会 (Shinano kyōikukai Suwa-bukai). (Arikazu is sometimes portrayed instead as the first priest to bear the title of ''ōhōri'' instead of ''misogi-no-hōri''.) Though officially the chief priest of the ''Kamisha'' and as incarnate deity, an object of worship, the Suwa ''ōhōri'' had little, if any, actual power, which rested in the hands of the Moriya ''jinchōkan'', with his unique ability to hear Mishaguji and call upon the god(s) to descend upon people or objects and his knowledge of special rituals, which were closely guarded secrets traditionally passed down via word of mouth only to the heir to the office.Moriya (1991), p. 5. In fact, it was by being possessed by Mishaguji (summoned by the ''jinchōkan'') during his investiture into the office that the Suwa ''ōhōri'' officially became a living deity.{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} {{ja icon}}Miyasaka (1987). p. 29. It was also forbidden for the ''ōhōri'' to ever leave Suwa; breaking this ban was thought to incur Mishaguji's wrath.{{cite web|title=諏訪大明神 (Suwa-daimyōjin)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E5%A4%A7%E6%98%8E%E7%A5%9E.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} {{ja icon}} ====Investiture ceremony==== The full rite of investiture into the office of ''ōhōri'' as practiced in the late medieval period originally involved the candidate - a seven- or eight-year-old boy from the Suwa clan - being brought before a [[maple]] (''kaede'') or ''[[Osmanthus heterophyllus|hiiragi]]'' tree west of the ''Gōdono'' (神殿), the ''ōhōri'''s residence during his term located in the precincts of one of the ''Kamisha'''s two component shrines, the ''Maemiya'' (前宮 'old shrine') in full regalia: wearing traditional makeup (''[[oshiroi]]'', ''[[ohaguro]]'', ''[[Rouge (cosmetics)|beni]]'' and ''[[Hikimayu|mayuzumi]]''), a dull yellow-green ''[[sokutai]]'' and a ''[[hakama]]'', with a crown (''kanmuri'') on his head.Miyasaka (1987). p. 28-29.Fujimori, Akira (1991). ''Ōhōri sokui no keshō-dōgu'' (大祝即位の化粧道具). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 37. {{ja icon}} Under the tree, known as ''Keikansha'' ([[wikt:鶏冠|鶏冠]]社) or ''Tosaka-no-miya'' ([[wikt:とさか|とさか]]の宮) among other names such as ''Kaede-no-miya'' (楓の宮) or ''Hiiragi-no-miya'' (柊の宮), was a flat rock known as the ''kaname-ishi'' (要石 'keystone'). During the ceremony, the Moriya ''jinchōkan'' led the candidate to the rock (then surrounded by a makeshift enclosure or hut), on which was laid a mat of reeds for the boy to sit on. With a secret incantation, the ''jinchōkan'' summoned Mishaguji - who as a [[nature spirit]] was believed to inhabit rocks and trees - to the ''kaname-ishi''; via the rock, Mishaguji was then believed to possess the child, thereby making him into a god and installing him into the office, which he held until he came of age (around fifteenMiyasaka (1992). p. 53.). ===As warriors: from the Kamakura period to the Sengoku period=== In the meantime, other male members of the clan aside from the ''ōhōri'' - who was forbidden to step outside the boundaries of the region while he served as priest - began to take up arms and pursue military careers. By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]]. During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan of the ''Shimosha'' which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601. ===Edo period onwards=== [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the Moriya clan's estate grounds in [[Chino, Nagano|Chino City]], Nagano.]]Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方'''). All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML}} {{ja icon}} Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control. The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', Hiroshi (諏方弘), the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.{{cite web|title=最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} {{ja icon}} ==See also== *[[Takeminakata]] *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Moreya]] *[[Suwa Domain]] *[[Suwa taisha]] *[[Suwa Province]] *[[Takeda Shingen]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} [[Category:Japanese clans]]

(see 'As ''ōhōri''' section below) - or the [[Seiwa Genji]] via Minamoto no Mitsuyasu (one of the sons of [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto]]).{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}}{{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=611|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}} It has also been theorized that historically, the Suwa may have actually originated from the Kanasashi clan (金刺氏), which in turn branched out from the clan of the provincial governors or ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko|kuni-no-miyatsuko]]'' of [[Shinano Province]] (the [[Yamato period|Yamato court]]'s representatives in the region) and were the chief priests or ''ōhōri'' of the ''Shimosha'', noting while the name 'Kanasashi' is already attested in sources from the [[Nara period|Nara]] and [[Heian period|Heian]] periods, the names 'Suwa' and 'Miwa' (神, also read as 'Shin' or 'Jin') do not appear in written records until the Kamakura period, around the same time sources begin to distinguish between the Suwa ''Kamisha'' and the ''Shimosha'' (earlier records still treat the shrines at Suwa more or less as a single entity).{{cite web|title=金刺氏 (Kanasashi-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/kanazasi.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}} Seemingly supporting this theory is the genealogical record of the Aso clan ([[:ja:阿蘇氏|阿蘇氏]]) of [[Aso Shrine]] (said to be related to the Kanasashi), which list both the Kanasashi and the Suwa as being of the same lineage.{{cite book|author=Rekishi REAL Henshūbu (歴史REAL編集部) (ed.)|title=Jinja to kodai gōzoku no nazo (神社と古代豪族の謎)|date=2016|publisher=Yosensha|isbn=978-4800308924|page=40}} {{ja icon}}{{cite book|last1=Miyasaka|first1=Mitsuaki|title=諏訪大社の御柱と年中行事 (Suwa-taisha no Onbashira to nenchu-gyōji)|date=1992|publisher=Kyōdo shuppansha|isbn=978-4876631780|pages=7}} {{ja icon}} ==History== ===As ''ōhōri''=== In antiquity, one member of the clan served as ''ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''ōhafuri'') of the ''Kamisha'', considered to be the visible embodiment of Suwa-myōjin himself and as such, [[Arahitogami|a living god]] (''arahitogami'') and an object of worship in his own right.{{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}} {{ja icon}}{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}} The ''ōhōri'', who traditionally assumed the position at a young age, was assisted by five priests headed by the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), a position occupied by the Moriya clan. Among the ''jinchōkan'''s roles were overseeing the ''Kamisha'''s rites and ceremonies in general, as well as summoning [[Mishaguji]] (a god or gods worshipped in Suwa since ancient times who is/are sometimes conflated with Takeminakata/Suwa-myōjin) to possess chosen individuals or inhabit inanimate objects during ceremonies when the presence of the god was called for.Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya-jinchō-ke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 4. {{ja icon}}Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In {{cite book|author1=Ueda|author2=Gorai|author3=Ōbayashi|author4=Miyasaka, M.|author5=Miyasaka, Y.|title=御柱祭と諏訪大社 (Onbashira-sai to Suwa-taisha)|location=Nagano|publisher=Chikuma Shobō|isbn=978-4480841810|pages=25-26}} {{ja icon}} According to legend, the very first priest - a boy by the age of eight - was chosen by Suwa-myōjin himself in a vision. The god, declaring that since he (the god) has no tangible physical form his priest (''hōri'') shall be worshipped instead as his embodiment, took off his robe and made the boy wear it, thus conferring both priesthood and divinity to him. Since then, the boy and his descendants who assumed the same office became known as ''misogi-no-hōri'' (御衣着祝 'priest (who) wears the sacred garment'), the precursor to the title of ''ōhōri''. The boy in the story has variously been identified with two semi-legendary individuals: Otoei (乙頴, also 'Otsuei'), also known as Kumako (神子 or 熊子), who supposedly lived around the time of [[Emperor Yōmei]] (585-587){{cite book|last1=Iida|first1=Kōtarō|title=諏訪史料 (Suwa shiryō), vol. 1|date=1898|page=5|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/765163/9}}Miyasaka (1992), pp. 7–11., and Arikazu (有員), claimed to have lived during the reign of [[Emperor Kanmu]] around the 9th century and sometimes even portrayed as the latter's son.{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=|page=8}}Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=u2Mf7Ef60FkC&pg=PA11 諏訪史年表] (Suwa Shinenpyō).'' Nagano: Suwa Kyōikukai. p. 11. {{ja icon}}神氏系図 (''Miwa-shi keizu'') in Miyachi, Naokazu (1931). [http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1076393/166 諏訪史 (Suwa-shi), vol. 2]. 信濃教育会諏訪部会 (Shinano kyōikukai Suwa-bukai). (Arikazu is sometimes portrayed instead as the first priest to bear the title of ''ōhōri'' instead of ''misogi-no-hōri''.) Though officially the chief priest of the ''Kamisha'' and as incarnate deity, an object of worship, the Suwa ''ōhōri'' had little, if any, actual power, which rested in the hands of the Moriya ''jinchōkan'', with his unique ability to hear Mishaguji and call upon the god(s) to descend upon people or objects and his knowledge of special rituals, which were closely guarded secrets traditionally passed down via word of mouth only to the heir to the office.Moriya (1991), p. 5. In fact, it was by being possessed by Mishaguji (summoned by the ''jinchōkan'') during his investiture into the office that the Suwa ''ōhōri'' officially became a living deity.{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} {{ja icon}}Miyasaka (1987). p. 29. It was also forbidden for the ''ōhōri'' to ever leave Suwa; breaking this ban was thought to incur Mishaguji's wrath.{{cite web|title=諏訪大明神 (Suwa-daimyōjin)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E5%A4%A7%E6%98%8E%E7%A5%9E.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} {{ja icon}} ====Investiture ceremony==== The full rite of investiture into the office of ''ōhōri'' as practiced in the late medieval period originally involved the candidate - a boy from the Suwa clan between the age of eight to fifteen - being brought before a [[maple]] (''kaede'') or ''[[Osmanthus heterophyllus|hiiragi]]'' tree west of the ''Gōdono'' (神殿), the ''ōhōri'''s residence during his term located in the precincts of one of the ''Kamisha'''s two component shrines, the ''Maemiya'' (前宮 'old shrine') in full regalia: wearing traditional makeup (''[[oshiroi]]'', ''[[ohaguro]]'', ''[[Rouge (cosmetics)|beni]]'' and ''[[Hikimayu|mayuzumi]]''), a dull yellow-green ''[[sokutai]]'' and a ''[[hakama]]'', with a crown (''kanmuri'') on his head.Miyasaka (1987). p. 28-29.Fujimori, Akira (1991). ''Ōhōri sokui no keshō-dōgu'' (大祝即位の化粧道具). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 37. {{ja icon}} Under the tree, known as ''Keikansha'' ([[wikt:鶏冠|鶏冠]]社) or ''Tosaka-no-miya'' ([[wikt:とさか|とさか]]の宮) among other names such as ''Kaede-no-miya'' (楓の宮) or ''Hiiragi-no-miya'' (柊の宮), was a flat rock known as the ''kaname-ishi'' (要石 'keystone'). During the ceremony, the Moriya ''jinchōkan'' led the candidate to the rock (then surrounded by a makeshift enclosure or hut), on which was laid a mat of reeds for the boy to sit on. With a secret incantation, the ''jinchōkan'' summoned Mishaguji - who as a [[nature spirit]] was believed to inhabit rocks and trees - to the ''kaname-ishi''; via the rock, Mishaguji was then believed to possess the child, thereby making him into a god and installing him into the office.Miyasaka (1992). p. 53. ===As warriors: from the Kamakura period to the Sengoku period=== In the meantime, other male members of the clan aside from the ''ōhōri'' - who was forbidden to step outside the boundaries of the region while he served as priest - began to take up arms and pursue military careers. By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]]. During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan of the ''Shimosha'' which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601. ===Edo period onwards=== [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the Moriya clan's estate grounds in [[Chino, Nagano|Chino City]], Nagano.]]Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方'''). All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML}} {{ja icon}} Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control. The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', Hiroshi (諏方弘), the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.{{cite web|title=最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} {{ja icon}} ==See also== *[[Takeminakata]] *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Moreya]] *[[Suwa Domain]] *[[Suwa taisha]] *[[Suwa Province]] *[[Takeda Shingen]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} [[Category:Japanese clans]]

{{Japanese name|Suwa}} {{Infobox Japanese clan |surname nihongo = 諏訪氏 |image = Image:Japanese crest Suwa Kajinoha(Black background).svg |image size = 140px |image caption = The emblem ([[Mon (badge)|''mon'']]) of the Suwa clan |home province =Suwa region (modern [[Chino, Nagano|Chino]], [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya]], [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa]] and [[Shimosuwa]]), [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] |parent house =Kanasashi clan? |titles =*''Ōhōri'' (''Ōhafuri'') of [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]] *Daimyō |founder = Unknown; see 'Ancestry' |final ruler = |current head = |founding year = |dissolution = |ruled until = |cadet branches = Suwa clan (諏方氏) (defunct)
Takatoo clan (高遠氏)
Hoshina clan (保科氏)
Chino clan (千野氏) }} The {{nihongo|'''Suwa clan'''|諏訪氏|Suwa-shi}} was a Japanese clan hailing from the area encompassing [[Lake Suwa]] in [[Shinano Province]] (modern-day [[Nagano Prefecture]]). Originally a family of priests who served at the [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]],{{cite book|last1=Bocking|first1=Brian|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|date=2005|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1135797393|page=142|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6d-RAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA142}} by the [[Kamakura period]] the clan - now named 'Suwa' - thrived as a prominent warrior clan with close ties to the [[Kamakura Shogunate|shogunate]]. Managing to survive the fall of both the Kamakura shogunate and the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] which it supported, its feud with local rival clans, and frequent clashes with its neighbor in [[Kai Province|Kai]], the [[Takeda clan]], during the [[Sengoku period]] (which ended in the extinction of the main family), the clan split into two branches by the [[Edo period]]: one ruling the [[Suwa Domain]] of [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] as [[daimyō]], with the other continuing to serve as priests of Suwa Grand Shrine. ==Ancestry== The clan's actual origins are shrouded in mystery. Legend claims that the clan is descended from the [[Kami|god]] of [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]], Suwa-myōjin, most often identified with [[Takeminakata]] of the ''[[Kojiki]]'', who was driven to exile in Suwa after his defeat at the hands of [[Takemikazuchi]], a messenger sent by the gods of [[Takama-ga-hara|heaven]] to claim the land held by his father [[Ōkuninushi]] in the name of the goddess [[Amaterasu]].{{cite book|last1=Chamberlain|first1=Basil|title=A translation of the "Ko-ji-ki" or Records of Ancient Matters|date=1882|url=http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj039.htm#fn_697}}{{cite book|author=J. Hackin|title=Asiatic Mythology: A Detailed Description and Explanation of the Mythologies of All the Great Nations of Asia|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HAZrFhvqnTkC&pg=PA395|year=1932|publisher=Asian Educational Services|isbn=978-81-206-0920-4|page=395}}{{cite book|author=Jean Herbert|title=Shinto: At the Fountainhead of Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sg_JBQAAQBAJ&pg=PT437|date=18 October 2010|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90376-2|page=437}} According to local tradition, Suwa-myōjin, a god who came from outside Suwa, fought against local gods who resisted his entry into the region such as [[Moreya]]. Upon their defeat and submission, Suwa-myōjin/Takeminakata then became the new chief god of Suwa,{{cite book|author=呉清恵|title=Cosmogonical Worldview of Jomon Pottery|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hxulspIN_2UC&pg=PA157|date=November 2011|publisher=株式会社　三恵社|isbn=978-4-88361-924-5|page=157}}{{cite book|author=Michael Ashkenazi|title=Handbook of Japanese Mythology|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gqs-y9R2AekC&pg=PA267|date=1 January 2003|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-57607-467-1|pages=267–268}} enshrined with his consort Yasakatome in Suwa Grand Shrine, a complex of four shrines grouped into two sites: the Upper Shrine or ''Kamisha'' (上社) located south of [[Lake Suwa]], and the Lower Shrine or ''Shimosha'' (下社) on the northern side of the lake. Both Moreya and Suwa-myōjin are said to have subsequently become the ancestors of two locally-prominent clans which served as priests of the ''Kamisha'', the Moriya (守矢氏) and the Suwa clans, respectively.{{cite book|last1=Picken|first1=Stuart D.B.|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0810871724|page=288|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&pg=PA288}}{{cite web|title=Brochure of the Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (神長官守矢資料館のしおり)|url=http://www.komainu.org/nagano/chinosi/MishagujiSousha/siori.pdf}} {{ja icon}} Other claimed ancestors of the clan include the [[Emperor Kanmu]] - via a supposed son named Arikazu (see 'As ''ōhōri''' section below) - or the [[Seiwa Genji]] via Minamoto no Mitsuyasu (one of the sons of [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto]]).{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}}{{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, The god, declaring that since he (the god) has no tangible physical form his priest (''hōri'') shall be worshipped instead as his embodiment, took off his robe and made the boy wear it, thus conferring both priesthood and divinity to him. Since then, the boy and his descendants who assumed the same office became known as ''misogi-no-hōri'' (御衣着祝 'priest (who) wears the sacred garment'), the precursor to the title of ''ōhōri''. The boy in the story has variously been identified with two semi-legendary individuals: Otoei (乙頴, also 'Otsuei'), also known as Kumako (神子 or 熊子), who supposedly lived around the time of [[Emperor Yōmei]] (585-587){{cite book|last1=Iida|first1=Kōtarō|title=諏訪史料 (Suwa shiryō), vol. 1|date=1898|page=5|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/765163/9}}Miyasaka (1992), pp. 7–11., and Arikazu (有員), claimed to have lived during the reign of [[Emperor Kanmu]] around the 9th century and sometimes even portrayed as the latter's son.{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=|page=8}}Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=u2Mf7Ef60FkC&pg=PA11 諏訪史年表] (Suwa Shinenpyō).'' Nagano: Suwa Kyōikukai. p. 11. {{ja icon}}神氏系図 (''Miwa-shi keizu'') in Miyachi, Naokazu (1931). [http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1076393/166 諏訪史 (Suwa-shi), vol. 2]. 信濃教育会諏訪部会 (Shinano kyōikukai Suwa-bukai). (Arikazu is sometimes portrayed instead as the first priest to bear the title of ''ōhōri'' instead of ''misogi-no-hōri''.) Though officially the chief priest of the ''Kamisha'' and as incarnate deity, an object of worship, the Suwa ''ōhōri'' had little, if any, actual power, which rested in the hands of the Moriya ''jinchōkan'', with his unique ability to hear Mishaguji and call upon the god(s) to descend upon people or objects and his knowledge of special rituals, which were closely guarded secrets traditionally passed down via word of mouth only to the heir to the office.Moriya (1991), p. 5. In fact, it was by being possessed by Mishaguji (summoned by the ''jinchōkan'') during his investiture into the office that the Suwa ''ōhōri'' officially became a living deity.{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} {{ja icon}}Miyasaka (1987). p. 29. It was also forbidden for the ''ōhōri'' to ever leave Suwa; breaking this ban was thought to incur Mishaguji's wrath.{{cite web|title=諏訪大明神 (Suwa-daimyōjin)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E5%A4%A7%E6%98%8E%E7%A5%9E.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} {{ja icon}} ====Investiture ceremony==== The full rite of investiture into the office of ''ōhōri'' as practiced in the late medieval period originally involved the candidate - a boy from the Suwa clan between the age of eight to fifteen - being brought before a [[maple]] (''kaede'') or ''[[Osmanthus heterophyllus|hiiragi]]'' tree west of the ''Gōdono'' (神殿), the ''ōhōri'''s residence during his term located in the precincts of one of the ''Kamisha'''s two component shrines, the ''Maemiya'' (前宮 'old shrine') in full regalia: wearing traditional makeup (''[[oshiroi]]'', ''[[ohaguro]]'', ''[[Rouge (cosmetics)|beni]]'' and ''[[Hikimayu|mayuzumi]]''), a dull yellow-green ''[[sokutai]]'' and a ''[[hakama]]'', with a crown (''kanmuri'') on his head.Miyasaka (1987). p. 28-29.Fujimori, Akira (1991). ''Ōhōri sokui no keshō-dōgu'' (大祝即位の化粧道具). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 37. {{ja icon}} Under the tree, known as ''Keikansha'' ([[wikt:鶏冠|鶏冠]]社) or ''Tosaka-no-miya'' ([[wikt:とさか|とさか]]の宮) among other names such as ''Kaede-no-miya'' (楓の宮) or ''Hiiragi-no-miya'' (柊の宮), was a flat rock known as the ''kaname-ishi'' (要石 'keystone'). During the ceremony, the Moriya ''jinchōkan'' led the candidate to the rock (then surrounded by a makeshift enclosure or hut), on which was laid a mat of reeds for the boy to sit on. With a secret incantation, the ''jinchōkan'' summoned Mishaguji - who as a [[nature spirit]] was believed to inhabit rocks and trees - to the ''kaname-ishi''; via the rock, Mishaguji was then believed to possess the child, thereby making him into a god and installing him into the office.Miyasaka (1992). p. 53. ===As warriors: from the Heian period to the Sengoku period=== In the meantime, other male members of the clan aside from the ''ōhōri'' - who was forbidden to step outside the boundaries of the region, as well as coming into contact with sources of impurity such as the flesh and blood of men or horses - began to pursue military careers. One of the first recorded warriors from the clan was Tamenaka (為仲), a son of the ''ōhōri'' Tamenobu (為信). Tamenaka served under [[Minamoto no Yoshiie]] during the [[Zenkunen War]] (1051-1063) under the orders of his father, who could not participate due to the ban on the ''ōhōri'' leaving Suwa. He then also participated in the later [[Gosannen War]] of the 1080s (again under Yoshiie), this time despite opposition from his family due to him already inheriting the position of ''ōhōri'' at the time. His eventual suicide out of shame after his subordinates had a violent quarrel with [[Minamoto no Yoshimitsu]]'s men during a feast held by the latter was considered to be divine punishment for his violation of the ban.Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). pp. 23-24.{{cite web|title=源氏御家人としての諏訪氏|url=http://rarememory.justhpbs.jp/kama/na.htm#%E5%BE%8C%E4%B8%89%E5%B9%B4%E3%81%AE%E5%BD%B9%E3%81%AE%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E7%82%BA%E4%BB%B2%E3%81%AE%E5%8E%BB%E5%B0%B1|website=信州歴史散歩}}{{cite book|last1=Miyachi|first1=Naokazu|title=諏訪史 第二卷 前編 (Suwa-shi, vol. 2, part 1)|date=1931|publisher=Shinano kyōikukai Suwa-bukai|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=4hBVjsO2GOgC|pages=274-275}} {{ja icon}} By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]]. During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan of the ''Shimosha'' which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601. ===Edo period onwards=== [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the Moriya clan's estate grounds in [[Chino, Nagano|Chino City]], Nagano.]]Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方'''). All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML}} {{ja icon}} Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control. The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', Hiroshi (諏方弘), the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.{{cite web|title=最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} {{ja icon}} ==See also== *[[Takeminakata]] *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Moreya]] *[[Suwa Domain]] *[[Suwa taisha]] *[[Suwa Province]] *[[Takeda Shingen]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} [[Category:Japanese clans]]

{{Japanese name|Suwa}} {{Infobox Japanese clan |surname nihongo = 諏訪氏 |image = Image:Japanese crest Suwa Kajinoha(Black background).svg |image size = 140px |image caption = The emblem ([[Mon (badge)|''mon'']]) of the Suwa clan |home province =Suwa region (modern [[Chino, Nagano|Chino]], [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya]], [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa]] and [[Shimosuwa]]), [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] |parent house =Kanasashi clan? |titles =*''Ōhōri'' (''Ōhafuri'') of [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]] *Daimyō |founder = Unknown; see 'Ancestry' |final ruler = |current head = |founding year = |dissolution = |ruled until = |cadet branches = Suwa clan (諏方氏) (defunct)
Takatoo clan (高遠氏)
Hoshina clan (保科氏)
Chino clan (千野氏) }} The {{nihongo|'''Suwa clan'''|諏訪氏|Suwa-shi}} was a Japanese clan hailing from the area encompassing [[Lake Suwa]] in [[Shinano Province]] (modern-day [[Nagano Prefecture]]). Originally a family of priests who served at the [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]],{{cite book|last1=Bocking|first1=Brian|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|date=2005|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1135797393|page=142|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6d-RAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA142}} by the [[Kamakura period]] the clan - now named 'Suwa' - thrived as a prominent warrior clan with close ties to the [[Kamakura Shogunate|shogunate]]. Managing to survive the fall of both the Kamakura shogunate and the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] which it supported, its feud with local rival clans, and frequent clashes with its neighbor in [[Kai Province|Kai]], the [[Takeda clan]], during the [[Sengoku period]] (which ended in the extinction of the main family), the clan split into two branches by the [[Edo period]]: one ruling the [[Suwa Domain]] of [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] as [[daimyō]], with the other continuing to serve as priests of Suwa Grand Shrine. ==Ancestry== The clan's actual origins are shrouded in mystery. Legend claims that the clan is descended from the [[Kami|god]] of [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]], Suwa-myōjin, most often identified with [[Takeminakata]] of the ''[[Kojiki]]'', who was driven to exile in Suwa after his defeat at the hands of [[Takemikazuchi]], a messenger sent by the gods of [[Takama-ga-hara|heaven]] to claim the land held by his father [[Ōkuninushi]] in the name of the goddess [[Amaterasu]].{{cite book|last1=Chamberlain|first1=Basil|title=A translation of the "Ko-ji-ki" or Records of Ancient Matters|date=1882|url=http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj039.htm#fn_697}}{{cite book|author=J. Hackin|title=Asiatic Mythology: A Detailed Description and Explanation of the Mythologies of All the Great Nations of Asia|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HAZrFhvqnTkC&pg=PA395|year=1932|publisher=Asian Educational Services|isbn=978-81-206-0920-4|page=395}}{{cite book|author=Jean Herbert|title=Shinto: At the Fountainhead of Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sg_JBQAAQBAJ&pg=PT437|date=18 October 2010|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90376-2|page=437}} According to local tradition, Suwa-myōjin, a god who came from outside Suwa, fought against local gods who resisted his entry into the region such as [[Moreya]]. Upon their defeat and submission, Suwa-myōjin/Takeminakata then became the new chief god of Suwa,{{cite book|author=呉清恵|title=Cosmogonical Worldview of Jomon Pottery|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hxulspIN_2UC&pg=PA157|date=November 2011|publisher=株式会社　三恵社|isbn=978-4-88361-924-5|page=157}}{{cite book|author=Michael Ashkenazi|title=Handbook of Japanese Mythology|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gqs-y9R2AekC&pg=PA267|date=1 January 2003|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-57607-467-1|pages=267–268}} enshrined with his consort Yasakatome in Suwa Grand Shrine, a complex of four shrines grouped into two sites: the Upper Shrine or ''Kamisha'' (上社) located south of [[Lake Suwa]], and the Lower Shrine or ''Shimosha'' (下社) on the northern side of the lake. Both Moreya and Suwa-myōjin are said to have subsequently become the ancestors of two locally-prominent clans which served as priests of the ''Kamisha'', the Moriya (守矢氏) and the Suwa clans, respectively.{{cite book|last1=Picken|first1=Stuart D.B.|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0810871724|page=288|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&pg=PA288}}{{cite web|title=Brochure of the Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (神長官守矢資料館のしおり)|url=http://www.komainu.org/nagano/chinosi/MishagujiSousha/siori.pdf}} {{ja icon}} Other claimed ancestors of the clan include the [[Emperor Kanmu]] - via a supposed son named Arikazu (see 'As ''ōhōri''' section below) - or the [[Seiwa Genji]] via Minamoto no Mitsuyasu (one of the sons of [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto]]).{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}}{{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=611|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}} It has also been theorized that historically, the Suwa may have actually originated from the Kanasashi clan (金刺氏), which in turn branched out from the clan of the provincial governors or ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko|kuni-no-miyatsuko]]'' of [[Shinano Province]] (the [[Yamato period|Yamato court]]'s representatives in the region) and were the chief priests or ''ōhōri'' of the ''Shimosha'', noting while the name 'Kanasashi' is already attested in sources from the [[Nara period|Nara]] and [[Heian period|Heian]] periods, the names 'Suwa' and 'Miwa' (神, also read as 'Shin' or 'Jin') do not appear in written records until the Kamakura period, around the same time sources begin to distinguish between the Suwa ''Kamisha'' and the ''Shimosha'' (earlier records still treat the shrines at Suwa more or less as a single entity).{{cite web|title=金刺氏 (Kanasashi-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/kanazasi.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}} Seemingly supporting this theory is the genealogical record of the Aso clan ([[:ja:阿蘇氏|阿蘇氏]]) of [[Aso Shrine]] (said to be related to the Kanasashi), which list both the Kanasashi and the Suwa as being of the same lineage.{{cite book|author=Rekishi REAL Henshūbu (歴史REAL編集部) (ed.)|title=Jinja to kodai gōzoku no nazo (神社と古代豪族の謎)|date=2016|publisher=Yosensha|isbn=978-4800308924|page=40}} {{ja icon}}{{cite book|last1=Miyasaka|first1=Mitsuaki|title=諏訪大社の御柱と年中行事 (Suwa-taisha no Onbashira to nenchu-gyōji)|date=1992|publisher=Kyōdo shuppansha|isbn=978-4876631780|pages=7}} {{ja icon}} ==History== ===As ''ōhōri''=== In antiquity, one member of the clan served as ''ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''ōhafuri'') of the ''Kamisha'', considered to be the visible embodiment of Suwa-myōjin himself and as such, [[Arahitogami|a living god]] (''arahitogami'') and an object of worship in his own right.{{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}} {{ja icon}}{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}} The ''ōhōri'', who traditionally assumed the position at a young age, was assisted by five priests headed by the ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), a position occupied by the Moriya clan. Among the ''jinchōkan'''s roles were overseeing the ''Kamisha'''s rites and ceremonies in general, as well as summoning [[Mishaguji]] (a god or gods worshipped in Suwa since ancient times who is/are sometimes conflated with Takeminakata/Suwa-myōjin) to possess chosen individuals or inhabit inanimate objects during ceremonies when the presence of the god was called for.Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya-jinchō-ke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 4. {{ja icon}}Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In {{cite book|author1=Ueda|author2=Gorai|author3=Ōbayashi|author4=Miyasaka, M.|author5=Miyasaka, Y.|title=御柱祭と諏訪大社 (Onbashira-sai to Suwa-taisha)|location=Nagano|publisher=Chikuma Shobō|isbn=978-4480841810|pages=25-26}} {{ja icon}} According to legend, the very first priest - a boy by the age of eight - was chosen by Suwa-myōjin himself in a vision. The god, declaring that since he (the god) has no tangible physical form his priest (''hōri'') shall be worshipped instead as his embodiment, took off his robe and made the boy wear it, thus conferring both priesthood and divinity to him. Since then, the boy and his descendants who assumed the same office became known as ''misogi-no-hōri'' (御衣着祝 'priest (who) wears the sacred garment'), the precursor to the title of ''ōhōri''. The boy in the story has variously been identified with two semi-legendary individuals: Otoei (乙頴, also 'Otsuei'), also known as Kumako (神子 or 熊子), who supposedly lived around the time of [[Emperor Yōmei]] (585-587){{cite book|last1=Iida|first1=Kōtarō|title=諏訪史料 (Suwa shiryō), vol. 1|date=1898|page=5|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/765163/9}}Miyasaka (1992), pp. 7–11., and Arikazu (有員), claimed to have lived during the reign of [[Emperor Kanmu]] around the 9th century and sometimes even portrayed as the latter's son.{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=|page=8}}Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=u2Mf7Ef60FkC&pg=PA11 諏訪史年表] (Suwa Shinenpyō).'' Nagano: Suwa Kyōikukai. p. 11. {{ja icon}}神氏系図 (''Miwa-shi keizu'') in Miyachi, Naokazu (1931). [http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1076393/166 諏訪史 (Suwa-shi), vol. 2]. 信濃教育会諏訪部会 (Shinano kyōikukai Suwa-bukai). (Arikazu is sometimes portrayed instead as the first priest to bear the title of ''ōhōri'' instead of ''misogi-no-hōri''.) It was also forbidden for the ''ōhōri'' to ever leave Suwa; breaking this ban was thought to incur Mishaguji's wrath.{{cite web|title=諏訪大明神 (Suwa-daimyōjin)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E5%A4%A7%E6%98%8E%E7%A5%9E.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} {{ja icon}} ====Investiture ceremony==== The full rite of investiture into the office of ''ōhōri'' as practiced in the late medieval period originally involved the candidate - a boy from the Suwa clan between the age of eight to fifteen - being brought before a [[maple]] (''kaede'') or ''[[Osmanthus heterophyllus|hiiragi]]'' tree west of the ''Gōdono'' (神殿), the ''ōhōri'''s residence during his term located in the precincts of one of the ''Kamisha'''s two component shrines, the ''Maemiya'' (前宮 'old shrine') in full regalia: wearing traditional makeup (''[[oshiroi]]'', ''[[ohaguro]]'', ''[[Rouge (cosmetics)|beni]]'' and ''[[Hikimayu|mayuzumi]]''), a dull yellow-green ''[[sokutai]]'' and a ''[[hakama]]'', with a crown (''kanmuri'') on his head.Miyasaka (1987). p. 28-29.Fujimori, Akira (1991). ''Ōhōri sokui no keshō-dōgu'' (大祝即位の化粧道具). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 37. {{ja icon}} Under the tree, known as ''Keikansha'' ([[wikt:鶏冠|鶏冠]]社) or ''Tosaka-no-miya'' ([[wikt:とさか|とさか]]の宮) among other names such as ''Kaede-no-miya'' (楓の宮) or ''Hiiragi-no-miya'' (柊の宮), was a flat rock known as the ''kaname-ishi'' (要石 'keystone'). During the ceremony, the Moriya ''jinchōkan'' led the candidate to the rock (then surrounded by a makeshift enclosure or hut), on which was laid a mat of reeds for the boy to sit on. With a secret incantation, the ''jinchōkan'' summoned Mishaguji - who as a [[nature spirit]] was believed to inhabit rocks and trees - to the ''kaname-ishi''; via the rock, Mishaguji was then believed to possess the child, thereby making him into a god and installing him into the office.Miyasaka (1992). p. 53. ===As warriors: from the Heian period to the Sengoku period=== In the meantime, other male members of the clan aside from the ''ōhōri'' - who cannot step outside the boundaries of the region, as well as come into contact with sources of impurity such as the flesh and blood of men or horses - began to pursue military careers. One of the first recorded warriors from the clan was Tamenaka (為仲), a son of then ''ōhōri'' Tamenobu (為信). Tamenaka served under [[Minamoto no Yoshiie]] during the [[Zenkunen War]] (1051-1063) under the orders of his father, who could not participate himself due to his priestly status. He then also served again under Yoshiie in the later [[Gosannen War]] of the 1080s, this time despite opposition from his family due to him already inheriting the position of ''ōhōri'' from Tamenobu in the interim between the two wars. Tamenaka's eventual suicide out of shame after his subordinates had a violent quarrel with [[Minamoto no Yoshimitsu]]'s men during a feast held by the latter was considered to be divine punishment for his violation of the ban.Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). pp. 23-24.{{cite web|title=源氏御家人としての諏訪氏|url=http://rarememory.justhpbs.jp/kama/na.htm#%E5%BE%8C%E4%B8%89%E5%B9%B4%E3%81%AE%E5%BD%B9%E3%81%AE%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E7%82%BA%E4%BB%B2%E3%81%AE%E5%8E%BB%E5%B0%B1|website=信州歴史散歩}}{{cite book|last1=Miyachi|first1=Naokazu|title=諏訪史 第二卷 前編 (Suwa-shi, vol. 2, part 1)|date=1931|publisher=Shinano kyōikukai Suwa-bukai|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=4hBVjsO2GOgC|pages=274-275}} {{ja icon}} Due to the circumstances of his father's death, Tamenaka's son, Tamemori (為盛) did not inherit the office of ''ōhōri'', it instead passing in succession to Tamenaka's three younger brothers, two of whom died within mere days of their investiture. It would be the youngest brother, Tamesada (為貞), who would turn out to successfully pass down the priesthood to his progeny. By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]]. During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan of the ''Shimosha'' which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601. ===Edo period onwards=== [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the Moriya clan's estate grounds in [[Chino, Nagano|Chino City]], Nagano.]]Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方'''). All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML}} {{ja icon}} Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control. The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', Hiroshi (諏方弘), the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.{{cite web|title=最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} {{ja icon}} ==See also== *[[Takeminakata]] *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Moreya]] *[[Suwa Domain]] *[[Suwa taisha]] *[[Suwa Province]] *[[Takeda Shingen]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} [[Category:Japanese clans]]
