{{Japanese name|Suwa}} {{Infobox Japanese clan |surname nihongo = 諏訪氏 |image = Image:Japanese crest Suwa Kajinoha(Black background).svg |image size = 140px |image caption = The emblem ([[Mon (badge)|''mon'']]) of the Suwa clan |home province =Suwa region (modern [[Chino, Nagano|Chino]], [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya]], [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa]] and [[Shimosuwa]]), [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] |parent house =Kanasashi clan? |titles =*''Ōhōri'' (''Ōhafuri'') of [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]] *Daimyō |founder = Unknown; see 'Ancestry' |final ruler = |current head = |founding year = |dissolution = |ruled until = |cadet branches = Suwa clan (諏方氏) (defunct)
Takatoo clan (高遠氏)
Hoshina clan (保科氏)
Chino clan (千野氏) }} The '''Suwa clan''' (諏訪氏 ''Suwa-shi''), also known as the '''Miwa clan''' (神氏 ''Miwa-shi''; also read as ''Jin'' or ''Shin'') was a Japanese clan hailing from the area encompassing [[Lake Suwa]] in [[Shinano Province]] (modern-day [[Nagano Prefecture]]). Originally a family of priests who served at the [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]],{{cite book|last1=Bocking|first1=Brian|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|date=2005|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1135797393|page=142|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6d-RAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA142}} by the [[Kamakura period]] the clan - now named 'Suwa' - thrived as a prominent warrior clan with close ties to the [[Kamakura Shogunate|shogunate]]. Managing to survive the fall of both the Kamakura shogunate and the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] which it supported, its feud with local rival clans, and frequent clashes with its neighbor in [[Kai Province|Kai]], the [[Takeda clan]], during the [[Sengoku period]] (which ended in the extinction of the main family), the clan split into two branches by the [[Edo period]]: one ruling the [[Suwa Domain]] of [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] as [[daimyō]], with the other continuing to serve as priests of Suwa Grand Shrine. ==Ancestry== [[File:Suwa-myojin.png|thumb|left|Suwa Daimyōjin as depicted in the ''[[Butsuzōzui]]'' (originally published 1690).]] Although the Suwa clan, who were the high priests of one of the component shrines of [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]], traditionally regarded themselves to be the descendants of the shrine's [[Kami|deity]], Suwa [[Myōjin]] (also known as [[Takeminakata]]),{{cite book|last1=Picken|first1=Stuart D.B.|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0810871724|page=288|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&pg=PA288}} the clan's actual historical origins are shrouded in mystery. While the ''[[Kojiki]]'' portrays Takeminakata as a son of the god [[Ōkuninushi]] driven to exile in Suwa after his defeat at the hands of [[Takemikazuchi|a messenger]] sent by the gods of [[Takama-ga-hara|heaven]] to [[Kuni-yuzuri|claim the land]] held by his father in the name of the goddess [[Amaterasu]],{{cite book|last1=Chamberlain|first1=Basil|title=A translation of the "Ko-ji-ki" or Records of Ancient Matters|date=1882|url=http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj039.htm#fn_697}}{{cite book|author=J. Hackin|title=Asiatic Mythology: A Detailed Description and Explanation of the Mythologies of All the Great Nations of Asia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HAZrFhvqnTkC&pg=PA395|year=1932|publisher=Asian Educational Services|isbn=978-81-206-0920-4|page=395}}{{cite book|author=Jean Herbert|title=Shinto: At the Fountainhead of Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sg_JBQAAQBAJ&pg=PT437|date=18 October 2010|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90376-2|page=437}}{{cite book |author=Michael Ashkenazi|title=Handbook of Japanese Mythology|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gqs-y9R2AekC&pg=PA267|date=1 January 2003 |publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-57607-467-1|pages=267–268}} other (often conflicting) origin stories regarding the god of Suwa Shrine portray him in a different light. In some stories, Suwa Myōjin is a conqueror who subdued a number of local deities who resisted him, one of them being the god [[Moreya]],{{cite book|author=呉清恵|title=Cosmogonical Worldview of Jomon Pottery |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hxulspIN_2UC&pg=PA157|date=November 2011|publisher=株式会社　三恵社|isbn=978-4-88361-924-5|page=157}} who is subsequently said to have become the ancestor of the Moriya (守矢氏) clan, one of the priestly families who served the Suwa lineage of high priests.Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya Jinchō-ke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). pp. 2–3.''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' (神長守矢氏系譜), in {{cite book|editor=Suwa Kyōikukai (諏訪教育会)|title=諏訪史料叢書 巻28 (Suwa shiryō-sōsho, vol. 28)|date=1931|location=Suwa|publisher=Suwa Kyōikukai|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1185913/24}} {{ja icon}} In another myth, the god is portrayed as a being with no physical form who chose an eight-year-old boy to become his priest and [[Arahitogami|living incarnation]] (see 'As ''ōhōri''' section below).Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=u2Mf7Ef60FkC&pg=PA11 諏訪史年表] (Suwa Shinenpyō).'' Nagano: Suwa Kyōikukai. p. 11.{{ja icon}}{{cite web|title=大祝有員 (Ōhōri Arikazu)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030504.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa Clan)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=|page=8}}{{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}} {{ja icon}} Although this first priest of the Suwa deity and eventual founder of the Suwa clan is traditionally claimed to be a semi-legendary individual from the [[Heian period]] named Arikazu (有員), one genealogical record of the Suwa clan discovered in 1884Ihara (2008). p. 261. portrays Arikazu as a descendant of an earlier priest named Kumako (神子 or 熊子).''Ōhōri-bon Jinshi Keizu'' (大祝本 神氏系図), cited in {{cite book|last1=Kanai|first1=Tenbi|title=Suwa-shinkō-shi (諏訪信仰史)|date=1982|publisher=Meicho Shuppan|pages=107, 190}} Seemingly corroborating this information is a genealogy of the Aso (阿蘇) clan of [[Aso Shrine]] in [[Kyushu]], in which Kumako (神子), also named Otoei (乙頴), is recorded as a son of the [[Yamato period|Yamato]]-appointed [[kuni no miyatsuko|provincial governor]] (''kuni no miyatsuko'') of [[Shinano Province]] during the time of [[Emperor Yōmei]] (585-587), Mase-gimi (麻背君), a.k.a. Iotari (五百足).''Ihon Asoshi Keizu'' (異本阿蘇氏系図), cited in Kanai (1982). p. 109. Recent reappraisals of these two genealogies (particularly that concerning the Aso genealogy), however, have cast doubt on their authenticity and reliability as historical sources.Ihara (2008). pp. 260-262.{{cite web|author=Fukushima, Masaki (福島正樹)|title=信濃古代の通史叙述をめぐって (Shinano kodai no tsūshi jojutsu wo megutte)|url=http://user1.matsumoto.ne.jp/~fukusima/yamakawa.htm|website=科野太郎の古代・中世史の部屋|accessdate=2017-09-24}}{{cite journal|author1=Itō, Rintarō (伊藤麟太朗)|title=所謂『阿蘇氏系図』について (Iwayuru 'Aso-shi Keizu' ni tsuite)|journal=Shinano (信濃)|date=1994|volume=46|issue=8|pages=696-697|publisher=Shinano Shigakukai (信濃史学会)}}{{cite journal|author1=Murasaki, Machiko (村崎真智子)|title=異本阿蘇氏系図試論 (Ihon Aso-shi keizu shiron)|journal=Hito, mono, kotoba no jinruigaku: Kokubu Naoichi Hakushi beiju kinen ronbunshū (ヒト・モノ・コトバの人類学. 国分直一博士米寿記念論文集)|date=1996|pages=202-218|publisher=Keiyūsha (慶友社)}}{{cite book|author1=Asoshina, Yasuo (阿蘇品 保夫)|title=阿蘇社と大宮司―中世の阿蘇 (Aso-sha to Daiguji: chusei no Aso)|date=1999|publisher=Ichinomiya-machi (一の宮町)|isbn=978-4877550462}} For a contrary viewpoint, cf. {{cite web|author1=Hōga, Yoshio (宝賀寿男)|title=村崎真智子氏論考「異本阿蘇氏系図試論」等を読む|url=http://wwr2.ucom.ne.jp/hetoyc15/|date=2006}} Apart from these candidates, the clan has also been claimed to descend from the [[Seiwa Genji]] via Minamoto no Mitsuyasu (one of the sons of [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto]]).{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}}{{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=611|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}} ==The Suwa ''Ōhōri''== [[File:Suwa taisha Kamisha Maemiya , 諏訪大社 上社 前宮 - panoramio (13).jpg|thumb|''Kamisha Maemiya'', one of the two main shrines that comprise the Upper Shrine of Suwa]] In antiquity, a member of the clan served as the high priest or ''Ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''Ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''Ōhafuri'') of the Upper Shrine of Suwa (上社 ''Kamisha''), considered to be the visible embodiment of the Suwa deity himself and as such, [[Arahitogami|a living god]] and an object of worship in his own right.{{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}} {{ja icon}}{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}} The Suwa ''Ōhōri'', who traditionally assumed the position at a young age (between the ages of eight to fifteen), was assisted by five priests headed by the ''Jinchōkan'' (神長官), a position occupied by the Moriya clan. The ''Jinchōkan'' was responsible for overseeing the Upper Shrine's rites and ceremonies in general, many of which are centered around the worship of divine spirit(s) called [[Mishaguji]].Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya-jinchō-ke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 4. {{ja icon}}Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In {{cite book|author1=Ueda|author2=Gorai|author3=Ōbayashi|author4=Miyasaka, M.|author5=Miyasaka, Y.|title=御柱祭と諏訪大社 (Onbashira-sai to Suwa-taisha)|location=Nagano|publisher=Chikuma Shobō|isbn=978-4480841810|pages=25–26}} {{ja icon}} It has been observed that the religious atmosphere of Suwa is a syncretism of ancient indigenous beliefs and practices (e.g. Mishaguji worship) reorganized under a Yamato framework (i.e. the Suwa deity and the ''Ōhōri''), but with the local element still predominant. Though officially the Upper Shrine's chief priest and as incarnate deity, an object of worship, the Suwa ''Ōhōri'' had little, if any, actual power, which rested in the hands of the Moriya ''jinchōkan'', with his unique ability to hear the Mishaguji and call upon the god(s) to descend upon people or objects and his knowledge of special rituals, which were closely guarded secrets traditionally passed down via word of mouth only to the heir to the office.Moriya (1991), p. 5. In fact, it was due to the Mishaguji entering the candidate's body during his investiture into the office that the Suwa ''Ōhōri'' officially became a living deity.{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} {{ja icon}}Miyasaka (1987). p. 29. It was also forbidden for the ''ōhōri'' to ever leave Suwa; breaking this ban was thought to incur the wrath of the gods.{{cite web|title=諏訪大明神 (Suwa-daimyōjin)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E5%A4%A7%E6%98%8E%E7%A5%9E.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} {{ja icon}} ===Investiture ceremony=== The full rite of investiture into the office of ''ōhōri'' as practiced in the late medieval period originally involved the candidate - a boy from the Suwa clan between the age of eight to fifteen - being brought before a [[maple]] (''kaede'') or holly (''[[Osmanthus heterophyllus|hiiragi]]'') tree west of the ''Gōdono'' (神殿), the ''ōhōri'''s residence during his term located in the precincts of one of the Upper Shrine's two component shrines, the ''Maemiya'' (前宮 'old shrine'). Under the tree, known as ''Keikansha'' ([[wikt:鶏冠|鶏冠]]社) or ''Tosaka-no-miya'' ([[wikt:とさか|とさか]]の宮) among other names such as ''Kaede-no-miya'' (楓の宮) or ''Hiiragi-no-miya'' (柊の宮), was a flat rock known as the ''kaname-ishi'' (要石 'keystone'). During the ceremony, the Moriya ''jinchōkan'' led the candidate to the rock (then surrounded by a makeshift enclosure or hut), on which was laid a mat of reeds for the boy to sit on. After dressing the boy in full ritual attire - traditional makeup (''[[oshiroi]]'', ''[[ohaguro]]'', ''[[Rouge (cosmetics)|beni]]'' and ''[[Hikimayu|mayuzumi]]''), a dull yellow-green ''[[sokutai]]'', a ''[[hakama]]'', and a crown (''kanmuri'') - the ''jinchōkan'' summoned Mishaguji (who as a [[nature spirit]] was believed to inhabit rocks and trees) to the ''kaname-ishi'' with a secret incantation. Through the rock, Mishaguji was then believed to enter the child's body, thereby turning him into a god and installing him into the office.Miyasaka (1992). p. 53.Miyasaka (1987). p. 28-29.Fujimori, Akira (1991). ''Ōhōri sokui no keshō-dōgu'' (大祝即位の化粧道具). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 37. {{ja icon}} As time went on the ritual became increasingly simplified and later, was supposedly even omitted altogether, with the ''ōhōri'' simply assuming the position without any ceremony.{{cite web|title=大祝即位式場|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/zatugaku/sokui.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} ===Residence=== During his term of office, the ''ōhōri'' originally resided in a building near the Suwa ''Maemiya'' known as the ''Gōdono'' (神殿). Reflecting its being the residence of the ''ōhōri'' (considered a god incarnate), the ''Maemiya'' area and its vicinity was known during the Middle Ages as the ''Gōbara'' (神原), the 'god's field'.{{cite book|editor1-last=Tanigawa|editor1-first=Kenichi|title=Nihon no kamigami: Jinja to seichi, vol. 9: Mino, Hida, Shinano (日本の神々―神社と聖地〈9〉美濃・飛騨・信濃)|date=1987|publisher=Hakusuisha|isbn=978-4560025093|pages=138–139}} Should the ''ōhōri'' die while in office, his corpse was immediately brought to the presence of Suwa Myōjin (i.e. the shrine) where he was first ceremonially retired from office before being taken out of the shrine's precincts through a gate reserved solely for the purpose, the "unopened gate" (不明門 ''akazu-no-mon'') and buried in his clothes, with hair and beard unshaven - or later, as per Buddhist custom, [[Cremation|cremated]].{{cite web|title=諏訪大社本宮の「不明門」|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/zatugaku/akazu.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} By the early 17th century, the ''ōhōri'''s residence was moved from the ''Maemiya'' to [https://www.google.co.jp/maps/place/%E3%80%92392-0015+Nagano-ken,+Suwa-shi,+Nakasu,+%E5%A4%A7%E7%A5%9D%E5%B1%8B%E6%95%B7/@36.000373,138.1261382,18z/data=!4m5!3m4!1s0x601c56f08ec073dd:0x2f127865a478c42a!8m2!3d36.0003473!4d138.1271388 a place] in what is now Nakasu, [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa City]]. ==History== ===From the Heian period to the Sengoku period=== In the meantime, other male members of the clan aside from the ''ōhōri'' - who cannot step outside the boundaries of the region, as well as come into contact with sources of impurity such as the flesh and blood of men or horses - began to pursue military careers. One of the first recorded warriors from the clan was Tamenaka (為仲), a son of then ''ōhōri'' Tamenobu (為信). Tamenaka served under [[Minamoto no Yoshiie]] during the [[Zenkunen War]] (1051-1063) under the orders of his father, who could not participate himself due to his priestly status. He then also served again under Yoshiie in the later [[Gosannen War]] of the 1080s, this time despite opposition from his family due to him already inheriting the position of ''ōhōri'' from Tamenobu in the interim between the two wars. Tamenaka's eventual suicide out of shame after his subordinates had a violent quarrel with [[Minamoto no Yoshimitsu]]'s men during a feast held by the latter was considered to be divine punishment for his violation of the ban.Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). pp. 23-24.{{cite web|title=源氏御家人としての諏訪氏|url=http://rarememory.justhpbs.jp/kama/na.htm#%E5%BE%8C%E4%B8%89%E5%B9%B4%E3%81%AE%E5%BD%B9%E3%81%AE%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E7%82%BA%E4%BB%B2%E3%81%AE%E5%8E%BB%E5%B0%B1|website=信州歴史散歩}}{{cite book|last1=Miyachi|first1=Naokazu|title=諏訪史 第二卷 前編 (Suwa-shi, vol. 2, part 1)|date=1931|publisher=Shinano kyōikukai Suwa-bukai|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=4hBVjsO2GOgC|pages=274–275}} {{ja icon}} Due to the circumstances of his father's death, Tamenaka's son, Tamemori (為盛) did not inherit the office of ''ōhōri'', it instead passing in succession to Tamenaka's three younger brothers, two of whom died within mere days of their investiture. It would be the youngest brother, Tamesada (為貞), who would turn out to successfully pass down the priesthood to his progeny. By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]]. During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan of the ''Shimosha'' which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601. ===Edo period onwards=== [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the Moriya clan's estate grounds in [[Chino, Nagano|Chino City]], Nagano.]]Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方'''). All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML}} {{ja icon}} Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control. The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.{{cite web|title=最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} {{ja icon}} ==See also== *[[Takeminakata]] *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Moreya]] *[[Suwa Domain]] *[[Suwa taisha]] *[[Suwa Province]] *[[Takeda Shingen]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} [[Category:Japanese clans]]

{{Japanese name|Suwa}} {{Infobox Japanese clan |surname nihongo = 諏訪氏 |image = Image:Japanese crest Suwa Kajinoha(Black background).svg |image size = 140px |image caption = The emblem ([[Mon (badge)|''mon'']]) of the Suwa clan |home province =Suwa region (modern [[Chino, Nagano|Chino]], [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya]], [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa]] and [[Shimosuwa]]), [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] |parent house =Kanasashi clan? |titles =*''Ōhōri'' (''Ōhafuri'') of [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]] *Daimyō |founder = Unknown; see 'Ancestry' |final ruler = |current head = |founding year = |dissolution = |ruled until = |cadet branches = Suwa clan (諏方氏) (defunct)
Takatoo clan (高遠氏)
Hoshina clan (保科氏)
Chino clan (千野氏) }} The '''Suwa clan''' (諏訪氏 ''Suwa-shi''), also known as the '''Miwa clan''' (神氏 ''Miwa-shi''; also read as ''Jin'' or ''Shin'') was a Japanese clan hailing from the area encompassing [[Lake Suwa]] in [[Shinano Province]] (modern-day [[Nagano Prefecture]]). Originally a family of priests who served at the [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]],{{cite book|last1=Bocking|first1=Brian|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|date=2005|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1135797393|page=142|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6d-RAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA142}} by the [[Kamakura period]] it thrived as a prominent warrior clan with close ties to the [[Kamakura Shogunate|shogunate]]. Surviving the fall of both the Kamakura shogunate and the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] which it supported, its feud with local rival clans, and frequent clashes with its neighbor in [[Kai Province|Kai]], the [[Takeda clan]], during the [[Sengoku period]] (which ended in the extinction of the main family), the clan split into two branches by the [[Edo period]]: one ruling the [[Suwa Domain]] of [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] as [[daimyō]], with the other continuing to serve as priests of Suwa Grand Shrine. ==Ancestry== [[File:Suwa-myojin.png|thumb|left|Suwa Daimyōjin as depicted in the ''[[Butsuzōzui]]'' (originally published 1690).]] Although the Suwa clan, who were the high priests of one of the component shrines of [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]], traditionally regarded themselves to be the descendants of the shrine's [[Kami|deity]], Suwa [[Myōjin|Daimyōjin]] (also known as [[Takeminakata]]),{{cite book|last1=Picken|first1=Stuart D.B.|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0810871724|page=288|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&pg=PA288}} the clan's actual historical origins are shrouded in mystery. While the ''[[Kojiki]]'' portrays Takeminakata as a son of the god [[Ōkuninushi]] driven to exile in Suwa after his defeat at the hands of [[Takemikazuchi|a messenger]] sent by the gods of [[Takama-ga-hara|heaven]] to [[Kuni-yuzuri|claim the land]] held by his father in the name of the goddess [[Amaterasu]],{{cite book|last1=Chamberlain|first1=Basil|title=A translation of the "Ko-ji-ki" or Records of Ancient Matters|date=1882|url=http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj039.htm#fn_697}}{{cite book|author=J. Hackin|title=Asiatic Mythology: A Detailed Description and Explanation of the Mythologies of All the Great Nations of Asia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HAZrFhvqnTkC&pg=PA395|year=1932|publisher=Asian Educational Services|isbn=978-81-206-0920-4|page=395}}{{cite book|author=Jean Herbert|title=Shinto: At the Fountainhead of Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sg_JBQAAQBAJ&pg=PT437|date=18 October 2010|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90376-2|page=437}}{{cite book |author=Michael Ashkenazi|title=Handbook of Japanese Mythology|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gqs-y9R2AekC&pg=PA267|date=1 January 2003 |publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-57607-467-1|pages=267–268}} other (often conflicting) myths regarding the god of Suwa Shrine portray him in a different light. In some stories, Suwa Daimyōjin is a conqueror who subdued a number of local deities, one of them being the god [[Moreya]],{{cite book|author=呉清恵|title=Cosmogonical Worldview of Jomon Pottery |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hxulspIN_2UC&pg=PA157|date=November 2011|publisher=株式会社　三恵社|isbn=978-4-88361-924-5|page=157}} who is subsequently said to have become the ancestor of the Moriya (守矢氏) clan, one of the priestly families who served the Suwa lineage of high priests.Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya Jinchō-ke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). pp. 2–3.''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' (神長守矢氏系譜), in {{cite book|editor=Suwa Kyōikukai (諏訪教育会)|title=諏訪史料叢書 巻28 (Suwa shiryō-sōsho, vol. 28)|date=1931|location=Suwa|publisher=Suwa Kyōikukai|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1185913/24}} {{ja icon}} In another myth, the god is a being with no physical form who chose an eight-year-old boy to become his priest and [[Arahitogami|living incarnation]] (see 'As ''ōhōri''' section below).Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=u2Mf7Ef60FkC&pg=PA11 諏訪史年表] (Suwa Shinenpyō).'' Nagano: Suwa Kyōikukai. p. 11.{{ja icon}}{{cite web|title=大祝有員 (Ōhōri Arikazu)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030504.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa Clan)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=|page=8}}{{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}} {{ja icon}} Although this boy, who is said to have been the founding ancestor of the clan, is traditionally claimed to be a semi-legendary priest from the [[Heian period]] named Arikazu (有員), one genealogical record of the Suwa clan discovered in 1884Ihara (2008). p. 261. portrays Arikazu as a descendant of an earlier priest named Kumako (神子 or 熊子).''Ōhōri-bon Jinshi Keizu'' (大祝本 神氏系図), cited in {{cite book|last1=Kanai|first1=Tenbi|title=Suwa-shinkō-shi (諏訪信仰史)|date=1982|publisher=Meicho Shuppan|pages=107, 190}} Seemingly corroborating this information is a genealogy of the Aso (阿蘇) clan of [[Aso Shrine]] in [[Kyushu]], in which Kumako (神子), also named Otoei (乙頴), is recorded as a son of the [[Yamato period|Yamato]]-appointed [[kuni no miyatsuko|provincial governor]] (''kuni no miyatsuko'') of [[Shinano Province]] during the time of [[Emperor Yōmei]] (585-587), Mase-gimi (麻背君), a.k.a. Iotari (五百足).''Ihon Asoshi Keizu'' (異本阿蘇氏系図), cited in Kanai (1982). p. 109. Recent reappraisals of these two genealogies (particularly that concerning the Aso genealogy), however, have cast doubt on their authenticity and reliability as historical sources.Ihara (2008). pp. 260-262.{{cite web|author=Fukushima, Masaki (福島正樹)|title=信濃古代の通史叙述をめぐって (Shinano kodai no tsūshi jojutsu wo megutte)|url=http://user1.matsumoto.ne.jp/~fukusima/yamakawa.htm|website=科野太郎の古代・中世史の部屋|accessdate=2017-09-24}}{{cite journal|author1=Itō, Rintarō (伊藤麟太朗)|title=所謂『阿蘇氏系図』について (Iwayuru 'Aso-shi Keizu' ni tsuite)|journal=Shinano (信濃)|date=1994|volume=46|issue=8|pages=696-697|publisher=Shinano Shigakukai (信濃史学会)}}{{cite journal|author1=Murasaki, Machiko (村崎真智子)|title=異本阿蘇氏系図試論 (Ihon Aso-shi keizu shiron)|journal=Hito, mono, kotoba no jinruigaku: Kokubu Naoichi Hakushi beiju kinen ronbunshū (ヒト・モノ・コトバの人類学. 国分直一博士米寿記念論文集)|date=1996|pages=202-218|publisher=Keiyūsha (慶友社)}}{{cite book|author1=Asoshina, Yasuo (阿蘇品 保夫)|title=阿蘇社と大宮司―中世の阿蘇 (Aso-sha to Daiguji: chusei no Aso)|date=1999|publisher=Ichinomiya-machi (一の宮町)|isbn=978-4877550462}} For a contrary viewpoint, cf. {{cite web|author1=Hōga, Yoshio (宝賀寿男)|title=村崎真智子氏論考「異本阿蘇氏系図試論」等を読む|url=http://wwr2.ucom.ne.jp/hetoyc15/|date=2006}} Apart from these candidates, the clan has also been claimed to descend from the [[Seiwa Genji]] via Minamoto no Mitsuyasu (one of the sons of [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto]]).{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}}{{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=611|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}} ==The Suwa ''Ōhōri''== [[File:Suwa taisha Kamisha Maemiya , 諏訪大社 上社 前宮 - panoramio (13).jpg|thumb|''Kamisha Maemiya'', one of the two main shrines that comprise the Upper Shrine of Suwa. The Upper Shrine's high priest or ''Ōhōri'' resided in this area during the medieval period.]] In antiquity, the Suwa clan produced the Upper Shrine (上社 ''Kamisha'') of Suwa's high priest known as the ''Ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''Ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''Ōhafuri''), who was worshiped as [[Arahitogami|the living avatar]] of the shrine's deity during his period in office.{{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}} {{ja icon}}{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}} The ''Ōhōri'', who traditionally assumed the position at a young age (ideally between the ages of eight to fifteen), was assisted by five priests headed by the ''Jinchōkan'' (神長官) of the Moriya clan, who oversaw the Upper Shrine's religious rituals, many of which are centered around the worship of divine spirit(s) called [[Mishaguji]]. The ''Jinchōkan'' was believed to have the prerogative to [[Spirit possession|summon the Mishaguji onto individuals and objects]] whenever its presence was called for.Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya-jinchō-ke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 4. {{ja icon}}Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In {{cite book|author1=Ueda|author2=Gorai|author3=Ōbayashi|author4=Miyasaka, M.|author5=Miyasaka, Y.|title=御柱祭と諏訪大社 (Onbashira-sai to Suwa-taisha)|location=Nagano|publisher=Chikuma Shobō|isbn=978-4480841810|pages=25–26}} {{ja icon}} Though officially the Upper Shrine's chief priest and as incarnate deity, an object of worship, the Suwa ''Ōhōri'' had little, if any, actual power over the shrine's affairs, which rested in the hands of the Moriya ''Jinchōkan'', with his unique ability to hear the Mishaguji and call upon the god(s) to descend upon people or objects and his knowledge of closely guarded secret traditions passed down via word of mouth only to the heir to the office.Moriya (1991), p. 5. In fact, it was due to the Mishaguji possessing the ''Ōhōri'' during the investiture ceremony that he became a living deity.{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} {{ja icon}}Miyasaka (1987). p. 29. It was also forbidden for the ''Ōhōri'' to ever leave Suwa during his term of office under pain of divine punishment.{{cite web|title=諏訪大明神 (Suwa-daimyōjin)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E5%A4%A7%E6%98%8E%E7%A5%9E.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} {{ja icon}} ===Investiture ceremony=== The full rite of investiture into the office of ''Ōhōri'' as practiced in the late medieval period involved the candidate being brought before a [[maple]] (''kaede'') or holly (''[[Osmanthus heterophyllus|hiiragi]]'') tree west of the ''Gōdono'' (神殿), the ''Ōhōri'''s residence during his term located in the precincts of one of the Upper Shrine's two component shrines, the ''Maemiya'' (前宮 'old shrine'). Under the tree, known as ''Keikansha'' ([[wikt:鶏冠|鶏冠]]社) or ''Tosaka-no-miya'' ([[wikt:とさか|とさか]]の宮) among other names such as ''Kaede-no-miya'' (楓の宮) or ''Hiiragi-no-miya'' (柊の宮), was a flat rock known as thne ''kame-ishi'' (要石 'keystone'). During the ceremony, the''i''Mor''J''ya ''jinchōkan'' led the candidate to the rock (then surrounded by a makeshift enclosure or hut), on which was laid a mat of reeds for the boy to sit on. After dressing the boy in full ritual attire - traditional makeup (''[[oshiroi]]'', ''[[ohaguro]]'', ''[[Rouge (cosmetics)|beni]]'' and ''[[Hikimayu|mayuzumi]]''), a dull yellow-green ''[[sokutai]]'', a ''[[hakama]]'', and a crown (''kanmuri'') - the ''jinchōkan'' summoned Mishaguji (who as a [[nature spirit]] was believed to inhabit rocks and trees) to the ''kaname-ishi'' with a secret incantation. Through the rock, Mishaguji was then believed to enter the child's body, thereby turning him into a god and installing him into the office.Miyasaka (1992). p. 53.Miyasaka (1987). p. 28-29.Fujimori, Akira (1991). ''Ōhōri sokui no keshō-dōgu'' (大祝即位の化粧道具). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 37. {{ja icon}} As time went on the ritual became increasingly simplified and later, was supposedly even omitted altogether, with the ''ōhōri'' simply assuming the position without any ceremony.{{cite web|title=大祝即位式場|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/zatugaku/sokui.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} ===Residence=== During his term of office, the ''ōhōri'' originally resided in a building near the Suwa ''Maemiya'' known as the ''Gōdono'' (神殿). Reflecting its being the residence of the ''ōhōri'' (considered a god incarnate), the ''Maemiya'' area and its vicinity was known during the Middle Ages as the ''Gōbara'' (神原), the 'god's field'.{{cite book|editor1-last=Tanigawa|editor1-first=Kenichi|title=Nihon no kamigami: Jinja to seichi, vol. 9: Mino, Hida, Shinano (日本の神々―神社と聖地〈9〉美濃・飛騨・信濃)|date=1987|publisher=Hakusuisha|isbn=978-4560025093|pages=138–139}} Should the ''ōhōri'' die while in office, his corpse was immediately brought to the presence of Suwa Myōjin (i.e. the shrine) where he was first ceremonially retired from office before being taken out of the shrine's precincts through a gate reserved solely for the purpose, the "unopened gate" (不明門 ''akazu-no-mon'') and buried in his clothes, with hair and beard unshaven - or later, as per Buddhist custom, [[Cremation|cremated]].{{cite web|title=諏訪大社本宮の「不明門」|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/zatugaku/akazu.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} By the early 17th century, the ''ōhōri'''s residence was moved from the ''Maemiya'' to [https://www.google.co.jp/maps/place/%E3%80%92392-0015+Nagano-ken,+Suwa-shi,+Nakasu,+%E5%A4%A7%E7%A5%9D%E5%B1%8B%E6%95%B7/@36.000373,138.1261382,18z/data=!4m5!3m4!1s0x601c56f08ec073dd:0x2f127865a478c42a!8m2!3d36.0003473!4d138.1271388 a place] in what is now Nakasu, [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa City]]. ==History== ===From the Heian period to the Sengoku period=== In the meantime, other male members of the clan aside from the ''ōhōri'' - who cannot step outside the boundaries of the region, as well as come into contact with sources of impurity such as the flesh and blood of men or horses - began to pursue military careers. One of the first recorded warriors from the clan was Tamenaka (為仲), a son of then ''ōhōri'' Tamenobu (為信). Tamenaka served under [[Minamoto no Yoshiie]] during the [[Zenkunen War]] (1051-1063) under the orders of his father, who could not participate himself due to his priestly status. He then also served again under Yoshiie in the later [[Gosannen War]] of the 1080s, this time despite opposition from his family due to him already inheriting the position of ''ōhōri'' from Tamenobu in the interim between the two wars. Tamenaka's eventual suicide out of shame after his subordinates had a violent quarrel with [[Minamoto no Yoshimitsu]]'s men during a feast held by the latter was considered to be divine punishment for his violation of the ban.Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). pp. 23-24.{{cite web|title=源氏御家人としての諏訪氏|url=http://rarememory.justhpbs.jp/kama/na.htm#%E5%BE%8C%E4%B8%89%E5%B9%B4%E3%81%AE%E5%BD%B9%E3%81%AE%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E7%82%BA%E4%BB%B2%E3%81%AE%E5%8E%BB%E5%B0%B1|website=信州歴史散歩}}{{cite book|last1=Miyachi|first1=Naokazu|title=諏訪史 第二卷 前編 (Suwa-shi, vol. 2, part 1)|date=1931|publisher=Shinano kyōikukai Suwa-bukai|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=4hBVjsO2GOgC|pages=274–275}} {{ja icon}} Due to the circumstances of his father's death, Tamenaka's son, Tamemori (為盛) did not inherit the office of ''ōhōri'', it instead passing in succession to Tamenaka's three younger brothers, two of whom died within mere days of their investiture. It would be the youngest brother, Tamesada (為貞), who would turn out to successfully pass down the priesthood to his progeny. By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]]. During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan of the ''Shimosha'' which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601. ===Edo period onwards=== [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the Moriya clan's estate grounds in [[Chino, Nagano|Chino City]], Nagano.]]Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方'''). All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML}} {{ja icon}} Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control. The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.{{cite web|title=最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} {{ja icon}} ==See also== *[[Takeminakata]] *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Moreya]] *[[Suwa Domain]] *[[Suwa taisha|Suwa Taisha]] *[[Suwa Province]] *[[Takeda Shingen]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} [[Category:Japanese clans]]

{{Japanese name|Suwa}} {{Infobox Japanese clan |surname nihongo = 諏訪氏 |image = Image:Japanese crest Suwa Kajinoha(Black background).svg |image size = 140px |image caption = The emblem ([[Mon (badge)|''mon'']]) of the Suwa clan |home province =Suwa region (modern [[Chino, Nagano|Chino]], [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya]], [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa]] and [[Shimosuwa]]), [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] |parent house =Kanasashi clan? |titles =*''Ōhōri'' (''Ōhafuri'') of [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]] *Daimyō |founder = Unknown; see 'Ancestry' |final ruler = |current head = |founding year = |dissolution = |ruled until = |cadet branches = Suwa clan (諏方氏) (defunct)
Takatoo clan (高遠氏)
Hoshina clan (保科氏)
Chino clan (千野氏) }} The '''Suwa clan''' (諏訪氏 ''Suwa-shi''), also known as the '''Miwa clan''' (神氏 ''Miwa-shi''; also read as ''Jin'' or ''Shin'') was a Japanese clan hailing from the area encompassing [[Lake Suwa]] in [[Shinano Province]] (modern-day [[Nagano Prefecture]]). Originally a family of priests who served at the [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]],{{cite book|last1=Bocking|first1=Brian|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|date=2005|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1135797393|page=142|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6d-RAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA142}} by the [[Kamakura period]] it thrived as a prominent warrior clan with close ties to the [[Kamakura Shogunate|shogunate]]. Surviving the fall of both the Kamakura shogunate and the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] which it supported, its feud with local rival clans, and frequent clashes with its neighbor in [[Kai Province|Kai]], the [[Takeda clan]], during the [[Sengoku period]] (which ended in the extinction of the main family), the clan split into two branches by the [[Edo period]]: one ruling the [[Suwa Domain]] of [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] as [[daimyō]], with the other continuing to serve as priests of Suwa Grand Shrine. ==Ancestry== [[File:Suwa-myojin.png|thumb|left|Suwa Daimyōjin as depicted in the ''[[Butsuzōzui]]'' (originally published 1690).]] Although the Suwa clan, who were the high priests of one of the component shrines of [[Suwa taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]], traditionally regarded themselves to be the descendants of the shrine's [[Kami|deity]], Suwa [[Myōjin|Daimyōjin]] (also known as [[Takeminakata]]),{{cite book|last1=Picken|first1=Stuart D.B.|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0810871724|page=288|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&pg=PA288}} the clan's actual historical origins are shrouded in mystery. While the ''[[Kojiki]]'' portrays Takeminakata as a son of the god [[Ōkuninushi]] driven to exile in Suwa after his defeat at the hands of [[Takemikazuchi|a messenger]] sent by the gods of [[Takama-ga-hara|heaven]] to [[Kuni-yuzuri|claim the land]] held by his father in the name of the goddess [[Amaterasu]],{{cite book|last1=Chamberlain|first1=Basil|title=A translation of the "Ko-ji-ki" or Records of Ancient Matters|date=1882|url=http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj039.htm#fn_697}}{{cite book|author=J. Hackin|title=Asiatic Mythology: A Detailed Description and Explanation of the Mythologies of All the Great Nations of Asia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HAZrFhvqnTkC&pg=PA395|year=1932|publisher=Asian Educational Services|isbn=978-81-206-0920-4|page=395}}{{cite book|author=Jean Herbert|title=Shinto: At the Fountainhead of Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sg_JBQAAQBAJ&pg=PT437|date=18 October 2010|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90376-2|page=437}}{{cite book |author=Michael Ashkenazi|title=Handbook of Japanese Mythology|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gqs-y9R2AekC&pg=PA267|date=1 January 2003 |publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-57607-467-1|pages=267–268}} other (often conflicting) myths regarding the god of Suwa Shrine portray him in a different light. In some stories, Suwa Daimyōjin is a conqueror who subdued a number of local deities, one of them being the god [[Moreya]],{{cite book|author=呉清恵|title=Cosmogonical Worldview of Jomon Pottery |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hxulspIN_2UC&pg=PA157|date=November 2011|publisher=株式会社　三恵社|isbn=978-4-88361-924-5|page=157}} who is subsequently said to have become the ancestor of the Moriya (守矢氏) clan, one of the priestly families who served the Suwa lineage of high priests.Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya Jinchō-ke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). pp. 2–3.''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' (神長守矢氏系譜), in {{cite book|editor=Suwa Kyōikukai (諏訪教育会)|title=諏訪史料叢書 巻28 (Suwa shiryō-sōsho, vol. 28)|date=1931|location=Suwa|publisher=Suwa Kyōikukai|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1185913/24}} {{ja icon}} In another myth, the god is a being with no physical form who chose an eight-year-old boy to become his priest and [[Arahitogami|living incarnation]] (see 'As ''ōhōri''' section below).Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=u2Mf7Ef60FkC&pg=PA11 諏訪史年表] (Suwa Shinenpyō).'' Nagano: Suwa Kyōikukai. p. 11.{{ja icon}}{{cite web|title=大祝有員 (Ōhōri Arikazu)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030504.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa Clan)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{ja icon}}}}{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=|page=8}}{{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}} {{ja icon}} Although this boy, who is said to have been the founding ancestor of the clan, is traditionally claimed to be a semi-legendary priest from the [[Heian period]] named Arikazu (有員), one genealogical record of the Suwa clan discovered in 1884Ihara (2008). p. 261. portrays Arikazu as a descendant of an earlier priest named Kumako (神子 or 熊子).''Ōhōri-bon Jinshi Keizu'' (大祝本 神氏系図), cited in {{cite book|last1=Kanai|first1=Tenbi|title=Suwa-shinkō-shi (諏訪信仰史)|date=1982|publisher=Meicho Shuppan|pages=107, 190}} Seemingly corroborating this information is a genealogy of the Aso (阿蘇) clan of [[Aso Shrine]] in [[Kyushu]], in which Kumako (神子), also named Otoei (乙頴), is recorded as a son of the [[Yamato period|Yamato]]-appointed [[kuni no miyatsuko|provincial governor]] (''kuni no miyatsuko'') of [[Shinano Province]] during the time of [[Emperor Yōmei]] (585-587), Mase-gimi (麻背君), a.k.a. Iotari (五百足).''Ihon Asoshi Keizu'' (異本阿蘇氏系図), cited in Kanai (1982). p. 109. Recent reappraisals of these two genealogies (particularly that concerning the Aso genealogy), however, have cast doubt on their authenticity and reliability as historical sources.Ihara (2008). pp. 260-262.{{cite web|author=Fukushima, Masaki (福島正樹)|title=信濃古代の通史叙述をめぐって (Shinano kodai no tsūshi jojutsu wo megutte)|url=http://user1.matsumoto.ne.jp/~fukusima/yamakawa.htm|website=科野太郎の古代・中世史の部屋|accessdate=2017-09-24}}{{cite journal|author1=Itō, Rintarō (伊藤麟太朗)|title=所謂『阿蘇氏系図』について (Iwayuru 'Aso-shi Keizu' ni tsuite)|journal=Shinano (信濃)|date=1994|volume=46|issue=8|pages=696-697|publisher=Shinano Shigakukai (信濃史学会)}}{{cite journal|author1=Murasaki, Machiko (村崎真智子)|title=異本阿蘇氏系図試論 (Ihon Aso-shi keizu shiron)|journal=Hito, mono, kotoba no jinruigaku: Kokubu Naoichi Hakushi beiju kinen ronbunshū (ヒト・モノ・コトバの人類学. 国分直一博士米寿記念論文集)|date=1996|pages=202-218|publisher=Keiyūsha (慶友社)}}{{cite book|author1=Asoshina, Yasuo (阿蘇品 保夫)|title=阿蘇社と大宮司―中世の阿蘇 (Aso-sha to Daiguji: chusei no Aso)|date=1999|publisher=Ichinomiya-machi (一の宮町)|isbn=978-4877550462}} For a contrary viewpoint, cf. {{cite web|author1=Hōga, Yoshio (宝賀寿男)|title=村崎真智子氏論考「異本阿蘇氏系図試論」等を読む|url=http://wwr2.ucom.ne.jp/hetoyc15/|date=2006}} Apart from these candidates, the clan has also been claimed to descend from the [[Seiwa Genji]] via Minamoto no Mitsuyasu (one of the sons of [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto]]).{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)}} {{ja icon}}{{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=611|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}} ==The Suwa ''Ōhōri''== [[File:Suwa taisha Kamisha Maemiya , 諏訪大社 上社 前宮 - panoramio (13).jpg|thumb|''Kamisha Maemiya'', one of the two main shrines that comprise the Upper Shrine of Suwa. The Upper Shrine's high priest or ''Ōhōri'' resided in this area during the medieval period.]] In antiquity, the Suwa clan produced the Upper Shrine (上社 ''Kamisha'') of Suwa's high priest known as the ''Ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''Ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''Ōhafuri''), who was worshiped as [[Arahitogami|the living avatar]] of the shrine's deity during his period in office.{{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41}} {{ja icon}}{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}} The ''Ōhōri'', who traditionally assumed the position at a young age (ideally between the ages of eight to fifteen), was assisted by five priests headed by the ''Jinchōkan'' (神長官) of the Moriya clan, who oversaw the Upper Shrine's religious rituals, many of which are centered around the worship of divine spirit(s) called [[Mishaguji]]. The ''Jinchōkan'' was believed to have the prerogative to [[Spirit possession|summon the Mishaguji onto individuals and objects]] whenever its presence was called for.Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya-jinchō-ke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 4. {{ja icon}}Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In {{cite book|author1=Ueda|author2=Gorai|author3=Ōbayashi|author4=Miyasaka, M.|author5=Miyasaka, Y.|title=御柱祭と諏訪大社 (Onbashira-sai to Suwa-taisha)|location=Nagano|publisher=Chikuma Shobō|isbn=978-4480841810|pages=25–26}} {{ja icon}} Though officially the Upper Shrine's chief priest and as incarnate deity, an object of worship, the Suwa ''Ōhōri'' had little, if any, actual power over the shrine's affairs, which rested in the hands of the Moriya ''Jinchōkan'', with his unique ability to hear the Mishaguji and call upon the god(s) to descend upon people or objects and his knowledge of closely guarded secret traditions passed down via word of mouth only to the heir to the office.Moriya (1991), p. 5. In fact, it was due to the Mishaguji possessing the ''Ōhōri'' during the investiture ceremony that he became a living deity.{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} {{ja icon}}Miyasaka (1987). p. 29. It was also forbidden for the ''Ōhōri'' to ever leave Suwa during his term of office under pain of divine punishment.{{cite web|title=諏訪大明神 (Suwa-daimyōjin)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E5%A4%A7%E6%98%8E%E7%A5%9E.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)}} {{ja icon}} ===Investiture ceremony=== The full rite of investiture into the office of ''Ōhōri'' as practiced in the late medieval period involved the candidate being brought before a [[maple]] (''kaede'') or holly (''[[Osmanthus heterophyllus|hiiragi]]'') tree west of the ''Gōdono'' (神殿), the ''Ōhōri'''s residence during his term located in the precincts of one of the Upper Shrine's two component shrines, the ''Maemiya'' (前宮 'old shrine'). Under the tree, known as ''Keikansha'' ([[wikt:鶏冠|鶏冠]]社) or ''Tosaka-no-miya'' ([[wikt:とさか|とさか]]の宮) among other names such as ''Kaede-no-miya'' (楓の宮) or ''Hiiragi-no-miya'' (柊の宮), was a flat rock known as thne ''kame-ishi'' (要石 'keystone'). During the ceremony, the ''Jinchōkan'' led the candidate to the rock (then surrounded by a makeshift enclosure or hut), on which was laid a mat of reeds for the boy to sit on. After dressing the boy in full ritual attire - traditional makeup (''[[oshiroi]]'', ''[[ohaguro]]'', ''[[Rouge (cosmetics)|beni]]'' and ''[[Hikimayu|mayuzumi]]''), a dull yellow-green ''[[sokutai]]'', a ''[[hakama]]'', and a crown (''kanmuri'') - the ''jinchōkan'' summoned the Mishaguji (who as a [[nature spirit]] was believed to inhabit rocks and trees) to the ''kanameishi'' via a secret incantation. Through the rock, the Mishaguji was then believed to enter the child's body, thereby turning him into a [[Arahitogami|living god]].Miyasaka (1992). p. 53.Miyasaka (1987). p. 28-29.Fujimori, Akira (1991). ''Ōhōri sokui no keshō-dōgu'' (大祝即位の化粧道具). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 37. {{ja icon}} As time went on the ritual became increasingly simplified and later, was supposedly even omitted altogether, with the ''ōhōri'' simply assuming the position without any ceremony.{{cite web|title=大祝即位式場|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/zatugaku/sokui.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} ===Residence=== During his term of office, the ''ōhōri'' originally resided in a building near the Suwa ''Maemiya'' known as the ''Gōdono'' (神殿). Reflecting its being the residence of the ''ōhōri'' (considered a god incarnate), the ''Maemiya'' area and its vicinity was known during the Middle Ages as the ''Gōbara'' (神原), the 'god's field'.{{cite book|editor1-last=Tanigawa|editor1-first=Kenichi|title=Nihon no kamigami: Jinja to seichi, vol. 9: Mino, Hida, Shinano (日本の神々―神社と聖地〈9〉美濃・飛騨・信濃)|date=1987|publisher=Hakusuisha|isbn=978-4560025093|pages=138–139}} Should the ''ōhōri'' die while in office, his corpse was immediately brought to the presence of Suwa Myōjin (i.e. the shrine) where he was first ceremonially retired from office before being taken out of the shrine's precincts through a gate reserved solely for the purpose, the "unopened gate" (不明門 ''akazu-no-mon'') and buried in his clothes, with hair and beard unshaven - or later, as per Buddhist custom, [[Cremation|cremated]].{{cite web|title=諏訪大社本宮の「不明門」|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/zatugaku/akazu.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} By the early 17th century, the ''ōhōri'''s residence was moved from the ''Maemiya'' to [https://www.google.co.jp/maps/place/%E3%80%92392-0015+Nagano-ken,+Suwa-shi,+Nakasu,+%E5%A4%A7%E7%A5%9D%E5%B1%8B%E6%95%B7/@36.000373,138.1261382,18z/data=!4m5!3m4!1s0x601c56f08ec073dd:0x2f127865a478c42a!8m2!3d36.0003473!4d138.1271388 a place] in what is now Nakasu, [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa City]]. ==History== ===From the Heian period to the Sengoku period=== In the meantime, other male members of the clan aside from the ''ōhōri'' - who cannot step outside the boundaries of the region, as well as come into contact with sources of impurity such as the flesh and blood of men or horses - began to pursue military careers. One of the first recorded warriors from the clan was Tamenaka (為仲), a son of then ''ōhōri'' Tamenobu (為信). Tamenaka served under [[Minamoto no Yoshiie]] during the [[Zenkunen War]] (1051-1063) under the orders of his father, who could not participate himself due to his priestly status. He then also served again under Yoshiie in the later [[Gosannen War]] of the 1080s, this time despite opposition from his family due to him already inheriting the position of ''ōhōri'' from Tamenobu in the interim between the two wars. Tamenaka's eventual suicide out of shame after his subordinates had a violent quarrel with [[Minamoto no Yoshimitsu]]'s men during a feast held by the latter was considered to be divine punishment for his violation of the ban.Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). pp. 23-24.{{cite web|title=源氏御家人としての諏訪氏|url=http://rarememory.justhpbs.jp/kama/na.htm#%E5%BE%8C%E4%B8%89%E5%B9%B4%E3%81%AE%E5%BD%B9%E3%81%AE%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E7%82%BA%E4%BB%B2%E3%81%AE%E5%8E%BB%E5%B0%B1|website=信州歴史散歩}}{{cite book|last1=Miyachi|first1=Naokazu|title=諏訪史 第二卷 前編 (Suwa-shi, vol. 2, part 1)|date=1931|publisher=Shinano kyōikukai Suwa-bukai|url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=4hBVjsO2GOgC|pages=274–275}} {{ja icon}} Due to the circumstances of his father's death, Tamenaka's son, Tamemori (為盛) did not inherit the office of ''ōhōri'', it instead passing in succession to Tamenaka's three younger brothers, two of whom died within mere days of their investiture. It would be the youngest brother, Tamesada (為貞), who would turn out to successfully pass down the priesthood to his progeny. By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]]. During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan of the ''Shimosha'' which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601. ===Edo period onwards=== [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the Moriya clan's estate grounds in [[Chino, Nagano|Chino City]], Nagano.]]Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方'''). All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML}} {{ja icon}} Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control. The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.{{cite web|title=最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} {{ja icon}} ==See also== *[[Takeminakata]] *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Moreya]] *[[Suwa Domain]] *[[Suwa taisha|Suwa Taisha]] *[[Suwa Province]] *[[Takeda Shingen]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} [[Category:Japanese clans]]
