{{Short description|Japanese social class and samurai clan}} {{family name hatnote|Suwa|lang=Japanese}} {{Infobox Japanese clan |surname nihongo = 諏訪氏 |image = Japanese crest Suwa Kajinoha(White background).svg |image size = 150px |image caption = The emblem ([[Mon (badge)|''mon'']]) of the Suwa clan |home province = [[Shinano Province]] |parent house = Kanasashi clan?
Ōmiwa clan? |titles = High priest (''Ōhōri'') of the [[Suwa-taisha|Upper Suwa Shrine]]
''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[Takashima Domain]]
|founder = [[Takeminakata]] (legendary)
Historically unknown |final ruler = |current head = |founding year = Unknown |dissolution = |ruled until = 1871 ([[:en:Abolition of the han system|''han'' system]] and [[State Shinto#Great Promulgation Campaign|hereditary priesthood]] abolished) |cadet branches = Suwa clan (諏方氏) (defunct)
Takatoo clan (高遠氏)
Hoshina clan (保科氏)
Chino clan (千野氏) }} The {{nihongo|'''Suwa clan'''|諏訪氏|Suwa-shi}}, also known as the '''Jin''' or '''Miwa clan''' (神氏, ''Miwa [[Uji (clan)|uji]] / Miwa-shi'' or ''Jinshi'') was a Japanese ''[[Shake (social class)|shake]]'' and [[samurai]] family. Originating from the area encompassing [[Lake Suwa]] in [[Shinano Province]] (modern-day [[Nagano Prefecture]]), it was originally a family of priests who served at the [[Suwa-taisha|Upper Shrine of Suwa]] located on the southwestern side of the lake.{{cite book|last1=Bocking|first1=Brian|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|date=2005|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1135797393|page=142|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6d-RAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA142}} By the [[Kamakura period]], it thrived as a prominent samurai clan with close ties to the [[Kamakura Shogunate|shogunate]]. Surviving the fall of both the Kamakura shogunate and the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] which it supported, its feud with local rival clans, and frequent clashes with its neighbor in [[Kai Province|Kai]], the [[Takeda clan]], during the [[Sengoku period]] (which ended in the extinction of the main family), by the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] the clan had split into two branches: one ruling the [[Suwa Domain]] of [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] as ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'', with the other continuing to serve as priests of Suwa Shrine until the [[Meiji (era)|Meiji period]]. ==Ancestry== === In legend === [[File:Suwa Daimyōjin - 諏訪大明神.jpg|left|thumb|Suwa Daimyōjin ([[Takeminakata]]) wearing hunting gear. Religious rites centered around hunting and agriculture were an integral part of Suwa Shrine's ritual calendar in the medieval period.]] Although the Suwa, which was the high priestly lineage of the Upper Shrine (上社 ''Kamisha'') of Suwa, one of the component shrines of [[Suwa-taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]], traditionally regarded themselves to be the descendants of the shrine's [[Kami|deity]], [[Takeminakata]] (also known as Suwa [[Myōjin|Daimyōjin]]),{{cite book|last1=Picken|first1=Stuart D.B.|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|date=28 December 2010|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0810871724|page=288|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&pg=PA288}} the clan's actual historical origins are shrouded in mystery. In the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Kujiki|Sendai Kuji Hongi]]'', Takeminakata is portrayed as a son of the god [[Ōkuninushi]] who fled to Suwa after his defeat at the hands of the god [[Takemikazuchi]], who was sent by the gods of [[Takamagahara|heaven]] to [[Kuni-yuzuri|claim the land]] held by his father in the name of the goddess [[Amaterasu]].{{cite book|last1=Chamberlain|first1=Basil|title=A translation of the "Ko-ji-ki" or Records of Ancient Matters|date=1882|url=http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj039.htm#fn_697}}{{cite book|author=J. Hackin|title=Asiatic Mythology: A Detailed Description and Explanation of the Mythologies of All the Great Nations of Asia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HAZrFhvqnTkC&pg=PA395|year=1932|publisher=Asian Educational Services|isbn=978-81-206-0920-4|page=395}}{{cite book|author=Jean Herbert|title=Shinto: At the Fountainhead of Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sg_JBQAAQBAJ&pg=PT437|date=18 October 2010|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90376-2|page=437}}{{cite book |author=Michael Ashkenazi|title=Handbook of Japanese Mythology|url=https://archive.org/details/handbookofjapane0000ashk|url-access=registration|date=1 January 2003 |publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-57607-467-1|pages=[https://archive.org/details/handbookofjapane0000ashk/page/267 267]–268}} Other myths (mostly of medieval provenance), however, portray the Suwa deity in a different light. In one story, Suwa Daimyōjin is an interloper who wrested control of Suwa from the indigenous god [[Moriya|Moriya]],{{cite book|author=Oh|first=Amana ChungHae|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hxulspIN_2UC&pg=PA157|title=Cosmogonical Worldview of Jomon Pottery|date=November 2011|publisher=Sankeisha|isbn=978-4-88361-924-5|page=157}} the mythical ancestor of the Moriya (守矢氏) clan, one of the priestly families of the Upper Shrine.Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya Jinchō-ke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). pp. 2–3.''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' (神長守矢氏系譜), in {{cite book|editor=Suwa Kyōikukai (諏訪教育会)|title=諏訪史料叢書 巻28 (Suwa shiryō-sōsho, vol. 28)|date=1931|location=Suwa|publisher=Suwa Kyōikukai|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1185913/24|language=ja}} In another myth, the god is said to have chosen an eight-year-old boy to become his priest (祝, ''hōri''; [[Historical kana orthography|historical orthography]]: ''hafuri'') and [[Shintai|living incarnation]] by clothing the latter with his own garments. This boy is eventually said to have become the founding ancestor of the Suwa clan.Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=u2Mf7Ef60FkC&pg=PA11 諏訪史年表] (Suwa Shinenpyō).'' Nagano: Suwa Kyōikukai. p. 11.{{in lang|ja}}{{cite web|title=大祝有員 (Ōhōri Arikazu)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030504.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City |language=ja}}{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa Clan)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City |language=ja}}{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=|page=8}}{{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41|language=ja}} Medieval tradition usually identified a semi-legendary individual named Arikazu (有員), who is said to have lived in the early [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] during the reigns of the emperors [[Emperor Kanmu|Kanmu]] (reigned 781-806), [[:en:Emperor Heizei|Heizei]] (806-809), and [[:en:Emperor Saga|Saga]] (809-823), to be this child.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=u2Mf7Ef60FkC|title=諏訪史年表 (Suwa shinenpyō)|date=1938|publisher=Suwa Kyōikukai|editor=Suwa Kyōikukai|location=Nagano|page=11}}Miyasaka (1987). p. 35.{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa Clan)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{in lang|ja}}}} The ''[[Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba]]'' (1356) for example relates:
At the beginning of the god's [[Honji suijaku|manifestation]], he took off his robe, put them on an eight year old boy, and dubbed him 'great priest' (''Ōhōri''). The god declared, "I do not have a body and so make this priest (''hōri'') my body." This [boy] is Arikazu (有員), the priest of the sacred robe (御衣祝 ''Misogihōri''), the founding ancestor of the Miwa (Jin) clan.
However, a brief text attached to a genealogical record of the Suwa clan discovered in the ''Ōhōri'''s residence in 1884Ihara (2008). p. 261. instead portrays Arikazu as a descendant of Kumako (神子 or 熊子), a son of a ''[[kuni no miyatsuko]]'' (provincial governor) of [[Shinano Province]], who is claimed to have founded the Upper Shrine during the reign of [[:en:Emperor Yōmei|Emperor Yōmei]] (585-587).''Ōhōri-bon Jinshi Keizu'' (大祝本 神氏系図), cited in {{cite book|last1=Kanai|first1=Tenbi|title=Suwa-shinkō-shi (諏訪信仰史)|date=1982|publisher=Meicho Shuppan|pages=107, 190}}
When Kumako was eight years old, the revered deity appeared, took off his robe and put them on Kumako. After declaring, "I do not have a body and so make you my body," he disappeared. This [Kumako] is the ancestor of Arikazu of the Miwa (Jin) clan, the ''Misogihōri''. In the second year of Emperor Yōmei, Kumako built a sanctuary at the foot of the mountain at the southern side of the lake.
Another genealogical record, that of the [[Aso clan]] ([[:ja:阿蘇氏|阿蘇氏]]) of [[Aso Shrine]] in [[Kyushu]] (discovered in 1956), similarly identifies Otoei (乙頴) - there given the alias 'Kumako' - as the "''Ōhōri'' of the great deity of Suwa" (諏訪大神大祝) and narrates the same legend as those found above.''Ihon Asoshi Keizu'' (異本阿蘇氏系図), cited in Kanai (1982). p. 109. Recent reappraisals of these two genealogies, however, have cast doubt on their authenticity and reliability as historical sources.Ihara (2008). pp. 260-262.{{cite web|author=Fukushima, Masaki (福島正樹)|title=信濃古代の通史叙述をめぐって (Shinano kodai no tsūshi jojutsu o megutte)|url=http://user1.matsumoto.ne.jp/~fukusima/yamakawa.htm|access-date=2017-09-24|website=科野太郎の古代・中世史の部屋}}{{cite journal|author1=Itō, Rintarō (伊藤麟太朗)|title=所謂『阿蘇氏系図』について (Iwayuru 'Aso-shi Keizu' ni tsuite)|journal=Shinano (信濃)|date=1994|volume=46|issue=8|pages=696–697|publisher=Shinano Shigakukai (信濃史学会)}}{{cite journal|author1=Murasaki, Machiko (村崎真智子)|title=異本阿蘇氏系図試論 (Ihon Aso-shi keizu shiron)|journal=Hito, mono, kotoba no jinruigaku: Kokubu Naoichi Hakushi beiju kinen ronbunshū (ヒト・モノ・コトバの人類学. 国分直一博士米寿記念論文集)|date=1996|pages=202–218|publisher=Keiyūsha (慶友社)}}{{cite book|author1=Asoshina, Yasuo (阿蘇品 保夫)|title=阿蘇社と大宮司―中世の阿蘇 (Aso-sha to Daiguji: chusei no Aso)|date=1999|publisher=Ichinomiya-machi (一の宮町)|isbn=978-4877550462}}For a contrary viewpoint, cf. {{cite web|author1=Hōga, Yoshio (宝賀寿男)|title=村崎真智子氏論考「異本阿蘇氏系図試論」等を読む|url=http://wwr2.ucom.ne.jp/hetoyc15/|date=2006}} Apart from these candidates, the clan has also been claimed to descend from the [[Seiwa Genji]] via Minamoto no Mitsuyasu (one of the sons of [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto]]).{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)|language=ja}}{{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=[https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete/page/n148 611]|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}} ==The Suwa ''Ōhōri''== [[File:Suwa taisha Kamisha Maemiya , 諏訪大社 上社 前宮 - panoramio (13).jpg|thumb|''Kamisha Maemiya'', one of the two main shrines that comprise the Upper Shrine of Suwa. The Upper Shrine's high priest or ''Ōhōri'' resided in this area during the medieval period.]] In antiquity, the Suwa clan produced the Upper Shrine (上社 ''Kamisha'') of Suwa's high priest known as the ''Ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''Ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''Ōhafuri''), who was worshiped as [[Arahitogami|the living avatar]] of the shrine's deity during his period in office.{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|year=1988|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}} The ''Ōhōri'', who traditionally assumed the position at a young age (ideally between the ages of eight to fifteen), was assisted [[Suwa taisha#Priests|by five priests]] headed by the ''Jinchōkan'' (神長官) of the Moriya clan, who oversaw the Upper Shrine's religious rituals, many of which are centered around the worship of [[List of agricultural gods|agricultural]] and [[List of fertility deities|fertility god(s)]] called [[Mishaguji]]. The ''Jinchōkan'' was believed to have the prerogative to [[Spirit possession|summon the Mishaguji onto individuals and objects]] whenever its presence was called for.Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya-jinchō-ke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 4. {{in lang|ja}}Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In {{cite book|author1=Ueda|author2=Gorai|author3=Ōbayashi|author4=Miyasaka, M.|author5=Miyasaka, Y.|title=御柱祭と諏訪大社 (Onbashira-sai to Suwa-taisha)|location=Nagano|publisher=Chikuma Shobō|isbn=978-4480841810|pages=25–26|language=ja}} Though officially the Upper Shrine's chief priest and as incarnate deity, an object of worship, the Suwa ''Ōhōri'' had little, if any, actual power over the shrine's affairs, which rested in the hands of the Moriya ''Jinchōkan'', with his unique relationship to the Mishaguji and his knowledge of closely guarded secret traditions passed down via word of mouth only to the heir to the office.Moriya (1991), p. 5. In fact, it was due to the ''Jinchōkan'' summoning the Mishaguji onto the ''Ōhōri'' during the investiture ceremony that the latter became a living deity.{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)|language=ja}}Miyasaka (1987). p. 29. ===Investiture ceremony=== The full rite of investiture into the office of ''Ōhōri'' as practiced in the late medieval period involved the candidate first undergoing a twenty-two day period of strict [[ritual purification]] in the ''Maemiya'' (前宮 'old shrine'), one of the Upper Shrine's two component shrines. During the day of the ceremony itself, the ''Jinchōkan'' led the candidate by the hand before a sacred tree west of the ''Gōdono'' (神殿), the ''Ōhōri'''s residence during his term located west of the ''Maemiya'', under which was a flat rock known as the ''kanameishi'' (要石 'keystone'). During the ceremony, this rock is surrounded a makeshift enclosure or hut and a mat of reeds was placed over it for the boy to sit on.Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 722. Inside this enclosure, the ''Jinchōkan'' dressed the boy in full ritual attire: traditional makeup (''[[oshiroi]]'', ''[[ohaguro]]'', ''[[Rouge (cosmetics)|beni]]'' and ''[[Hikimayu|mayuzumi]]''), a dull yellow-green ''[[sokutai]]'', a ''[[:en:Hakama|Hakama]]'', and a crown (''kanmuri'').Fujimori, Akira (1991). ''Ōhōri sokui no keshō-dōgu'' (大祝即位の化粧道具). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 37. {{in lang|ja}} The ''Jinchōkan'' then summoned the Mishaguji (who as a [[nature spirit]] was believed to manifest on rocks and trees) to the ''kanameishi'' via secret [[Mantra|incantations]]. Via the rock, the Mishaguji was then believed to enter the child's body, thereby turning him into a [[Arahitogami|living god]].Miyasaka (1992). p. 53.Miyasaka (1987). p. 28-29. [[File:Suwa taisha Kamisha Maemiya , 諏訪大社 上社 前宮 内御玉殿 - panoramio (2).jpg|thumb|left|The Uchi-no-mitama-den (内御玉殿)]] After being consecrated, the ''Ōhōri'' visited the various shrines of the Upper Shrine complex. In another shrine in the ''Maemiya'' area, the Uchi-no-mitama-den (内御霊殿), wherein was kept the sacred treasures of the Upper Shrine (a bell, a [[:en:Bronze mirror|mirror]], a [[:en:Bit (horse)|bit]] and a [[saddle]]) that were supposedly brought to the region by Suwa Daimyōjin himself,{{cite book|editor=Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai|title=諏訪市史 上巻 原始・古代・中世 (Suwa Shishi, vol. 1)|date=1995|location=Suwa|page=718|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/9572217}} the ''Ōhōri'' made a ritual declaration (申立 ''mōshitate'') that he has become the god's new 'body' and will henceforth avoid [[Kegare|impurity]].Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 696, 722-723. As time went on the ritual became increasingly simplified and later, was supposedly even omitted altogether, with the ''ōhōri'' simply assuming the position without any ceremony.{{cite web|title=大祝即位式場|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/zatugaku/sokui.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} ===Role=== During his term, the incumbent ''Ōhōri'' was treated as the physical manifestation of Suwa Daimyōjin. In 1186, [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] officially recognized the ''Ōhōri'' as the god's incarnation in a letter to his subordinates, declaring that the ''Ōhōri'''s orders are those of the god himself.Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 696. The ''Ōhōri'' was expected to live a life of ritual purity and was also forbidden to step outside the boundaries of Suwa region under pain of divine punishment.{{cite web|title=諏訪大明神 (Suwa-daimyōjin)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E5%A4%A7%E6%98%8E%E7%A5%9E.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)|language=ja}}Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 695. During his term of office, the ''Ōhōri'' originally resided in a building near the Suwa ''Maemiya'' known as the ''Gōdono'' (神殿). Reflecting its being the residence of an incarnate deity, the ''Maemiya'' area and its vicinity was known during the Middle Ages as the ''Gōbara'' (神原), the 'god's field'.{{cite book|editor1-last=Tanigawa|editor1-first=Kenichi|title=Nihon no kamigami: Jinja to seichi, vol. 9: Mino, Hida, Shinano (日本の神々―神社と聖地〈9〉美濃・飛騨・信濃)|date=1987|publisher=Hakusuisha|isbn=978-4560025093|pages=138–139}} Should an incumbent ''Ōhōri'' die while in office, his corpse was immediately brought before the Uchi-no-mitama-den where he was ceremonially retired - the idea being that the ''Ōhōri'''s spirit was temporarily deposited in the shrine until a new candidate was chosen.Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). pp. 718-719. Originally, the deceased priest was buried wearing hunting attire (such as that supposedly worn by Suwa Daimyōjin) and with hair and beard kept unshaven.Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. pp. 719. However, in 1465, with the death of then ''Ōhōri'' Yorinaga (頼長), the local priesthood began to adopt the Buddhist custom of [[:en:Cremation|Cremation]]. By the early 17th century, the ''Ōhōri'''s residence was moved from the ''Maemiya'' to [https://www.google.co.jp/maps/place/%E3%80%92392-0015+Nagano-ken,+Suwa-shi,+Nakasu,+%E5%A4%A7%E7%A5%9D%E5%B1%8B%E6%95%B7/@36.000373,138.1261382,18z/data=!4m5!3m4!1s0x601c56f08ec073dd:0x2f127865a478c42a!8m2!3d36.0003473!4d138.1271388 a place] in what is now Nakasu, [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa City]]. ==History== ===From the Heian period to the Sengoku period=== In the meantime, other male members of the clan aside from the ''ōhōri'' - who cannot step outside the boundaries of the region, as well as come into contact with sources of impurity such as the flesh and blood of men or horses - began to pursue military careers. One of the first recorded warriors from the clan was Tamenaka (為仲), a son of then ''ōhōri'' Tamenobu (為信). Tamenaka served under [[Minamoto no Yoshiie]] during the [[Zenkunen War]] (1051-1063) under the orders of his father, who could not participate himself due to his priestly status. He then also served again under Yoshiie in the later [[:en:Gosannen War|Gosannen War]] of the 1080s, this time despite opposition from his family due to him already inheriting the position of ''ōhōri'' from Tamenobu in the interim between the two wars. Tamenaka's eventual suicide out of shame after his subordinates had a violent quarrel with [[Minamoto no Yoshimitsu]]'s men during a feast held by the latter was considered to be divine punishment for his violation of the ban.Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). pp. 23-24.{{cite web|title=源氏御家人としての諏訪氏|url=http://rarememory.justhpbs.jp/kama/na.htm#%E5%BE%8C%E4%B8%89%E5%B9%B4%E3%81%AE%E5%BD%B9%E3%81%AE%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E7%82%BA%E4%BB%B2%E3%81%AE%E5%8E%BB%E5%B0%B1|website=信州歴史散歩}}{{cite book|last1=Miyachi|first1=Naokazu|title=諏訪史 第二卷 前編 (Suwa-shi, vol. 2, part 1)|date=1931|publisher=Shinano kyōikukai Suwa-bukai|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4hBVjsO2GOgC|pages=274–275|language=ja}} Due to the circumstances of his father's death, Tamenaka's son, Tamemori (為盛) did not inherit the office of ''ōhōri'', it instead passing in succession to Tamenaka's three younger brothers, two of whom died within mere days of their investiture. It would be the youngest brother, Tamesada (為貞), who would turn out to successfully pass down the priesthood to his progeny. By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[:en:Gokenin|Gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]]. During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan of the ''Shimosha'' which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[:en:Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige (daimyo)|Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601. ===Edo period onwards=== [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the Moriya clan's estate grounds in [[:en:Chino, Nagano|Chino City]], Nagano.]]Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[:en:Chinese characters|Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方'''). All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[:en:Han system|Han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML|language=ja}} Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control. The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.{{cite web|script-title=ja:最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人|language=ja}} ==See also== *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Moriya|Moreya]] *[[Suwa Domain]] *[[Suwa-taisha|Suwa Taisha]] *[[Suwa Province]] *[[Takeda Shingen]] *[[Takeminakata]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} {{Suwa Faith}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Pages without meta categories]] [[sn:Suwa clan]][[sn:Suwa clan]][[Category:japanese clans]] }} [[sn:Suwa clan]] [[en:Suwa clan]] [[Category:Pages without translation templates]] [[Category:Pages with valid en interwikis]] [[Category:pages with valid en interwikis 2]] [[de:Suwa (Klan)]] [[fa:خاندان سووا]] [[fr:Clan Suwa]] [[id:Klan Suwa]] [[it:Clan Suwa]] [[ja:諏訪氏]] [[ko:스와씨]] [[pt:Clã Suwa]] [[ru:Сува (род)]]

{{Short description|Japanese social class and samurai clan}} {{family name hatnote|Suwa|lang=Japanese}} {{Infobox Japanese clan |surname nihongo = 諏訪氏 |image = Japanese crest Suwa Kajinoha(White background).svg |image size = 150px |image caption = The emblem ([[Mon (badge)|''mon'']]) of the Suwa clan |home province = [[Shinano Province]] |parent house = Kanasashi clan?
Ōmiwa clan? |titles = High priest (''Ōhōri'') of the [[Suwa-taisha|Upper Suwa Shrine]]
''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[Takashima Domain]]
|founder = [[Takeminakata]] (legendary)
Historically unknown |final ruler = |current head = |founding year = Unknown |dissolution = |ruled until = 1871 ([[:en:Abolition of the han system|''han'' system]] and [[State Shinto#Great Promulgation Campaign|hereditary priesthood]] abolished) |cadet branches = Suwa clan (諏方氏) (defunct)
Takatoo clan (高遠氏)
Hoshina clan (保科氏)
Chino clan (千野氏) }} The {{nihongo|'''Suwa clan'''|諏訪氏|Suwa-shi}}, also known as the '''Jin''' or '''Miwa clan''' (神氏, ''Miwa [[Uji (clan)|uji]] / Miwa-shi'' or ''Jinshi'') was a Japanese ''[[Shake (social class)|shake]]'' and [[samurai]] family. Originating from the area encompassing [[Lake Suwa]] in [[Shinano Province]] (modern-day [[Nagano Prefecture]]), it was originally a family of priests who served at the [[Suwa-taisha|Upper Shrine of Suwa]] located on the southwestern side of the lake.{{cite book|last1=Bocking|first1=Brian|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|date=2005|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1135797393|page=142|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6d-RAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA142}} By the [[Kamakura period]], it thrived as a prominent samurai clan with close ties to the [[Kamakura Shogunate|shogunate]]. Surviving the fall of both the Kamakura shogunate and the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] which it supported, its feud with local rival clans, and frequent clashes with its neighbor in [[Kai Province|Kai]], the [[Takeda clan]], during the [[Sengoku period]] (which ended in the extinction of the main family), by the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] the clan had split into two branches: one ruling the [[Suwa Domain]] of [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] as ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'', with the other continuing to serve as priests of Suwa Shrine until the [[Meiji (era)|Meiji period]]. ==Ancestry== === In legend === [[File:Suwa Daimyōjin - 諏訪大明神.jpg|left|thumb|Suwa Daimyōjin ([[Takeminakata]]) wearing hunting gear. Religious rites centered around hunting and agriculture were an integral part of Suwa Shrine's ritual calendar in the medieval period.]] Although the Suwa, which was the high priestly lineage of the Upper Shrine (上社 ''Kamisha'') of Suwa, one of the component shrines of [[Suwa-taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]], traditionally regarded themselves to be the descendants of the shrine's [[Kami|deity]], [[Takeminakata]] (also known as Suwa [[Myōjin|Daimyōjin]]),{{cite book|last1=Picken|first1=Stuart D.B.|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|date=28 December 2010|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0810871724|page=288|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&pg=PA288}} the clan's actual historical origins are shrouded in mystery. In the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Kujiki|Sendai Kuji Hongi]]'', Takeminakata is portrayed as a son of the god [[Ōkuninushi]] who fled to Suwa after his defeat at the hands of the god [[Takemikazuchi]], who was sent by the gods of [[Takamagahara|heaven]] to [[Kuni-yuzuri|claim the land]] held by his father in the name of the goddess [[Amaterasu]].{{cite book|last1=Chamberlain|first1=Basil|title=A translation of the "Ko-ji-ki" or Records of Ancient Matters|date=1882|url=http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj039.htm#fn_697}}{{cite book|author=J. Hackin|title=Asiatic Mythology: A Detailed Description and Explanation of the Mythologies of All the Great Nations of Asia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HAZrFhvqnTkC&pg=PA395|year=1932|publisher=Asian Educational Services|isbn=978-81-206-0920-4|page=395}}{{cite book|author=Jean Herbert|title=Shinto: At the Fountainhead of Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sg_JBQAAQBAJ&pg=PT437|date=18 October 2010|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90376-2|page=437}}{{cite book |author=Michael Ashkenazi|title=Handbook of Japanese Mythology|url=https://archive.org/details/handbookofjapane0000ashk|url-access=registration|date=1 January 2003 |publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-57607-467-1|pages=[https://archive.org/details/handbookofjapane0000ashk/page/267 267]–268}} Other myths (mostly of medieval provenance), however, portray the Suwa deity in a different light. In one story, Suwa Daimyōjin is an interloper who wrested control of Suwa from the indigenous god [[Moriya|Moriya]],{{cite book|author=Oh|first=Amana ChungHae|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hxulspIN_2UC&pg=PA157|title=Cosmogonical Worldview of Jomon Pottery|date=November 2011|publisher=Sankeisha|isbn=978-4-88361-924-5|page=157}} the mythical ancestor of the Moriya (守矢氏) clan, one of the priestly families of the Upper Shrine.Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya Jinchō-ke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). pp. 2–3.''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' (神長守矢氏系譜), in {{cite book|editor=Suwa Kyōikukai (諏訪教育会)|title=諏訪史料叢書 巻28 (Suwa shiryō-sōsho, vol. 28)|date=1931|location=Suwa|publisher=Suwa Kyōikukai|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1185913/24|language=ja}} In another myth, the god is said to have chosen an eight-year-old boy to become his priest (祝, ''hōri''; [[Historical kana orthography|historical orthography]]: ''hafuri'') and [[Shintai|living incarnation]] by clothing the latter with his own garments. This boy is eventually said to have become the founding ancestor of the Suwa clan.Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=u2Mf7Ef60FkC&pg=PA11 諏訪史年表] (Suwa Shinenpyō).'' Nagano: Suwa Kyōikukai. p. 11.{{in lang|ja}}{{cite web|title=大祝有員 (Ōhōri Arikazu)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030504.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City |language=ja}}{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa Clan)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City |language=ja}}{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=|page=8}}{{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41|language=ja}} Medieval tradition usually identified a semi-legendary individual named Arikazu (有員), who is said to have lived in the early [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] during the reigns of the emperors [[Emperor Kanmu|Kanmu]] (reigned 781-806), [[:en:Emperor Heizei|Heizei]] (806-809), and [[:en:Emperor Saga|Saga]] (809-823), to be this child.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=u2Mf7Ef60FkC|title=諏訪史年表 (Suwa shinenpyō)|date=1938|publisher=Suwa Kyōikukai|editor=Suwa Kyōikukai|location=Nagano|page=11}}Miyasaka (1987). p. 35.{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa Clan)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{in lang|ja}}}} The ''[[Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba]]'' (1356) for example relates:
At the beginning of the god's [[Honji suijaku|manifestation]], he took off his robe, put them on an eight year old boy, and dubbed him 'great priest' (''Ōhōri''). The god declared, "I do not have a body and so make this priest (''hōri'') my body." This [boy] is Arikazu (有員), the priest of the sacred robe (御衣祝 ''Misogihōri''), the founding ancestor of the Miwa (Jin) clan.
However, a brief text attached to a genealogical record of the Suwa clan discovered in the ''Ōhōri'''s residence in 1884Ihara (2008). p. 261. instead portrays Arikazu as a descendant of Kumako (神子 or 熊子), a son of a ''[[kuni no miyatsuko]]'' (provincial governor) of [[Shinano Province]], who is claimed to have founded the Upper Shrine during the reign of [[:en:Emperor Yōmei|Emperor Yōmei]] (585-587).''Ōhōri-bon Jinshi Keizu'' (大祝本 神氏系図), cited in {{cite book|last1=Kanai|first1=Tenbi|title=Suwa-shinkō-shi (諏訪信仰史)|date=1982|publisher=Meicho Shuppan|pages=107, 190}}
When Kumako was eight years old, the revered deity appeared, took off his robe and put them on Kumako. After declaring, "I do not have a body and so make you my body," he disappeared. This [Kumako] is the ancestor of Arikazu of the Miwa (Jin) clan, the ''Misogihōri''. In the second year of Emperor Yōmei, Kumako built a sanctuary at the foot of the mountain at the southern side of the lake.
Another genealogical record, that of the [[Aso clan]] ([[:ja:阿蘇氏|阿蘇氏]]) of [[Aso Shrine]] in [[Kyushu]] (discovered in 1956), similarly identifies Otoei (乙頴) - there given the alias 'Kumako' - as the "''Ōhōri'' of the great deity of Suwa" (諏訪大神大祝) and narrates the same legend as those found above.''Ihon Asoshi Keizu'' (異本阿蘇氏系図), cited in Kanai (1982). p. 109. Recent reappraisals of these two genealogies, however, have cast doubt on their authenticity and reliability as historical sources.Ihara (2008). pp. 260-262.{{cite web|author=Fukushima, Masaki (福島正樹)|title=信濃古代の通史叙述をめぐって (Shinano kodai no tsūshi jojutsu o megutte)|url=http://user1.matsumoto.ne.jp/~fukusima/yamakawa.htm|access-date=2017-09-24|website=科野太郎の古代・中世史の部屋}}{{cite journal|author1=Itō, Rintarō (伊藤麟太朗)|title=所謂『阿蘇氏系図』について (Iwayuru 'Aso-shi Keizu' ni tsuite)|journal=Shinano (信濃)|date=1994|volume=46|issue=8|pages=696–697|publisher=Shinano Shigakukai (信濃史学会)}}{{cite journal|author1=Murasaki, Machiko (村崎真智子)|title=異本阿蘇氏系図試論 (Ihon Aso-shi keizu shiron)|journal=Hito, mono, kotoba no jinruigaku: Kokubu Naoichi Hakushi beiju kinen ronbunshū (ヒト・モノ・コトバの人類学. 国分直一博士米寿記念論文集)|date=1996|pages=202–218|publisher=Keiyūsha (慶友社)}}{{cite book|author1=Asoshina, Yasuo (阿蘇品 保夫)|title=阿蘇社と大宮司―中世の阿蘇 (Aso-sha to Daiguji: chusei no Aso)|date=1999|publisher=Ichinomiya-machi (一の宮町)|isbn=978-4877550462}}For a contrary viewpoint, cf. {{cite web|author1=Hōga, Yoshio (宝賀寿男)|title=村崎真智子氏論考「異本阿蘇氏系図試論」等を読む|url=http://wwr2.ucom.ne.jp/hetoyc15/|date=2006}} Apart from these candidates, the clan has also been claimed to descend from the [[Seiwa Genji]] via Minamoto no Mitsuyasu (one of the sons of [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto]]).{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)|language=ja}}{{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=[https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete/page/n148 611]|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}} ==The Suwa ''Ōhōri''== [[File:Suwa taisha Kamisha Maemiya , 諏訪大社 上社 前宮 - panoramio (13).jpg|thumb|''Kamisha Maemiya'', one of the two main shrines that comprise the Upper Shrine of Suwa. The Upper Shrine's high priest or ''Ōhōri'' resided in this area during the medieval period.]] In antiquity, the Suwa clan produced the Upper Shrine (上社 ''Kamisha'') of Suwa's high priest known as the ''Ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''Ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''Ōhafuri''), who was worshiped as [[Arahitogami|the living avatar]] of the shrine's deity during his period in office.{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|year=1988|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}} The ''Ōhōri'', who traditionally assumed the position at a young age (ideally between the ages of eight to fifteen), was assisted [[Suwa taisha#Priests|by five priests]] headed by the ''Jinchōkan'' (神長官) of the Moriya clan, who oversaw the Upper Shrine's religious rituals, many of which are centered around the worship of [[List of agricultural gods|agricultural]] and [[List of fertility deities|fertility god(s)]] called [[Mishaguji]]. The ''Jinchōkan'' was believed to have the prerogative to [[Spirit possession|summon the Mishaguji onto individuals and objects]] whenever its presence was called for.Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya-jinchō-ke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 4. {{in lang|ja}}Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In {{cite book|author1=Ueda|author2=Gorai|author3=Ōbayashi|author4=Miyasaka, M.|author5=Miyasaka, Y.|title=御柱祭と諏訪大社 (Onbashira-sai to Suwa-taisha)|location=Nagano|publisher=Chikuma Shobō|isbn=978-4480841810|pages=25–26|language=ja}} Though officially the Upper Shrine's chief priest and as incarnate deity, an object of worship, the Suwa ''Ōhōri'' had little, if any, actual power over the shrine's affairs, which rested in the hands of the Moriya ''Jinchōkan'', with his unique relationship to the Mishaguji and his knowledge of closely guarded secret traditions passed down via word of mouth only to the heir to the office.Moriya (1991), p. 5. In fact, it was due to the ''Jinchōkan'' summoning the Mishaguji onto the ''Ōhōri'' during the investiture ceremony that the latter became a living deity.{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)|language=ja}}Miyasaka (1987). p. 29. ===Investiture ceremony=== The full rite of investiture into the office of ''Ōhōri'' as practiced in the late medieval period involved the candidate first undergoing a twenty-two day period of strict [[ritual purification]] in the ''Maemiya'' (前宮 'old shrine'), one of the Upper Shrine's two component shrines. During the day of the ceremony itself, the ''Jinchōkan'' led the candidate by the hand before a sacred tree west of the ''Gōdono'' (神殿), the ''Ōhōri'''s residence during his term located west of the ''Maemiya'', under which was a flat rock known as the ''kanameishi'' (要石 'keystone'). During the ceremony, this rock is surrounded a makeshift enclosure or hut and a mat of reeds was placed over it for the boy to sit on.Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 722. Inside this enclosure, the ''Jinchōkan'' dressed the boy in full ritual attire: traditional makeup (''[[oshiroi]]'', ''[[ohaguro]]'', ''[[Rouge (cosmetics)|beni]]'' and ''[[:en:Hikimayu|mayuzumi]]''), a dull yellow-green ''[[sokutai]]'', a ''[[:en:Hakama|Hakama]]'', and a crown (''kanmuri'').Fujimori, Akira (1991). ''Ōhōri sokui no keshō-dōgu'' (大祝即位の化粧道具). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 37. {{in lang|ja}} The ''Jinchōkan'' then summoned the Mishaguji (who as a [[nature spirit]] was believed to manifest on rocks and trees) to the ''kanameishi'' via secret [[Mantra|incantations]]. Via the rock, the Mishaguji was then believed to enter the child's body, thereby turning him into a [[Arahitogami|living god]].Miyasaka (1992). p. 53.Miyasaka (1987). p. 28-29. [[File:Suwa taisha Kamisha Maemiya , 諏訪大社 上社 前宮 内御玉殿 - panoramio (2).jpg|thumb|left|The Uchi-no-mitama-den (内御玉殿)]] After being consecrated, the ''Ōhōri'' visited the various shrines of the Upper Shrine complex. In another shrine in the ''Maemiya'' area, the Uchi-no-mitama-den (内御霊殿), wherein was kept the sacred treasures of the Upper Shrine (a bell, a [[:en:Bronze mirror|mirror]], a [[:en:Bit (horse)|bit]] and a [[saddle]]) that were supposedly brought to the region by Suwa Daimyōjin himself,{{cite book|editor=Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai|title=諏訪市史 上巻 原始・古代・中世 (Suwa Shishi, vol. 1)|date=1995|location=Suwa|page=718|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/9572217}} the ''Ōhōri'' made a ritual declaration (申立 ''mōshitate'') that he has become the god's new 'body' and will henceforth avoid [[Kegare|impurity]].Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 696, 722-723. As time went on the ritual became increasingly simplified and later, was supposedly even omitted altogether, with the ''ōhōri'' simply assuming the position without any ceremony.{{cite web|title=大祝即位式場|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/zatugaku/sokui.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} ===Role=== During his term, the incumbent ''Ōhōri'' was treated as the physical manifestation of Suwa Daimyōjin. In 1186, [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] officially recognized the ''Ōhōri'' as the god's incarnation in a letter to his subordinates, declaring that the ''Ōhōri'''s orders are those of the god himself.Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 696. The ''Ōhōri'' was expected to live a life of ritual purity and was also forbidden to step outside the boundaries of Suwa region under pain of divine punishment.{{cite web|title=諏訪大明神 (Suwa-daimyōjin)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E5%A4%A7%E6%98%8E%E7%A5%9E.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)|language=ja}}Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 695. During his term of office, the ''Ōhōri'' originally resided in a building near the Suwa ''Maemiya'' known as the ''Gōdono'' (神殿). Reflecting its being the residence of an incarnate deity, the ''Maemiya'' area and its vicinity was known during the Middle Ages as the ''Gōbara'' (神原), the 'god's field'.{{cite book|editor1-last=Tanigawa|editor1-first=Kenichi|title=Nihon no kamigami: Jinja to seichi, vol. 9: Mino, Hida, Shinano (日本の神々―神社と聖地〈9〉美濃・飛騨・信濃)|date=1987|publisher=Hakusuisha|isbn=978-4560025093|pages=138–139}} Should an incumbent ''Ōhōri'' die while in office, his corpse was immediately brought before the Uchi-no-mitama-den where he was ceremonially retired - the idea being that the ''Ōhōri'''s spirit was temporarily deposited in the shrine until a new candidate was chosen.Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). pp. 718-719. Originally, the deceased priest was buried wearing hunting attire (such as that supposedly worn by Suwa Daimyōjin) and with hair and beard kept unshaven.Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. pp. 719. However, in 1465, with the death of then ''Ōhōri'' Yorinaga (頼長), the local priesthood began to adopt the Buddhist custom of [[:en:Cremation|Cremation]]. By the early 17th century, the ''Ōhōri'''s residence was moved from the ''Maemiya'' to [https://www.google.co.jp/maps/place/%E3%80%92392-0015+Nagano-ken,+Suwa-shi,+Nakasu,+%E5%A4%A7%E7%A5%9D%E5%B1%8B%E6%95%B7/@36.000373,138.1261382,18z/data=!4m5!3m4!1s0x601c56f08ec073dd:0x2f127865a478c42a!8m2!3d36.0003473!4d138.1271388 a place] in what is now Nakasu, [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa City]]. ==History== ===From the Heian period to the Sengoku period=== In the meantime, other male members of the clan aside from the ''ōhōri'' - who cannot step outside the boundaries of the region, as well as come into contact with sources of impurity such as the flesh and blood of men or horses - began to pursue military careers. One of the first recorded warriors from the clan was Tamenaka (為仲), a son of then ''ōhōri'' Tamenobu (為信). Tamenaka served under [[Minamoto no Yoshiie]] during the [[Zenkunen War]] (1051-1063) under the orders of his father, who could not participate himself due to his priestly status. He then also served again under Yoshiie in the later [[:en:Gosannen War|Gosannen War]] of the 1080s, this time despite opposition from his family due to him already inheriting the position of ''ōhōri'' from Tamenobu in the interim between the two wars. Tamenaka's eventual suicide out of shame after his subordinates had a violent quarrel with [[Minamoto no Yoshimitsu]]'s men during a feast held by the latter was considered to be divine punishment for his violation of the ban.Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). pp. 23-24.{{cite web|title=源氏御家人としての諏訪氏|url=http://rarememory.justhpbs.jp/kama/na.htm#%E5%BE%8C%E4%B8%89%E5%B9%B4%E3%81%AE%E5%BD%B9%E3%81%AE%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E7%82%BA%E4%BB%B2%E3%81%AE%E5%8E%BB%E5%B0%B1|website=信州歴史散歩}}{{cite book|last1=Miyachi|first1=Naokazu|title=諏訪史 第二卷 前編 (Suwa-shi, vol. 2, part 1)|date=1931|publisher=Shinano kyōikukai Suwa-bukai|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4hBVjsO2GOgC|pages=274–275|language=ja}} Due to the circumstances of his father's death, Tamenaka's son, Tamemori (為盛) did not inherit the office of ''ōhōri'', it instead passing in succession to Tamenaka's three younger brothers, two of whom died within mere days of their investiture. It would be the youngest brother, Tamesada (為貞), who would turn out to successfully pass down the priesthood to his progeny. By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[:en:Gokenin|Gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]]. During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan of the ''Shimosha'' which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[:en:Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige (daimyo)|Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601. ===Edo period onwards=== [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the Moriya clan's estate grounds in [[:en:Chino, Nagano|Chino City]], Nagano.]]Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[:en:Chinese characters|Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方'''). All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[:en:Han system|Han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML|language=ja}} Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control. The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.{{cite web|script-title=ja:最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人|language=ja}} ==See also== *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Moriya|Moreya]] *[[Suwa Domain]] *[[Suwa-taisha|Suwa Taisha]] *[[Suwa Province]] *[[Takeda Shingen]] *[[Takeminakata]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} {{Suwa Faith}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Pages without meta categories]] [[sn:Suwa clan]][[sn:Suwa clan]][[Category:japanese clans]] }} [[sn:Suwa clan]] [[en:Suwa clan]] [[Category:Pages without translation templates]] [[Category:Pages with valid en interwikis]] [[Category:pages with valid en interwikis 2]] [[de:Suwa (Klan)]] [[fa:خاندان سووا]] [[fr:Clan Suwa]] [[id:Klan Suwa]] [[it:Clan Suwa]] [[ja:諏訪氏]] [[ko:스와씨]] [[pt:Clã Suwa]] [[ru:Сува (род)]]

{{Short description|Japanese social class and samurai clan}} {{family name hatnote|Suwa|lang=Japanese}} {{Infobox Japanese clan |surname nihongo = 諏訪氏 |image = Japanese crest Suwa Kajinoha(White background).svg |image size = 150px |image caption = The emblem ([[Mon (badge)|''mon'']]) of the Suwa clan |home province = [[Shinano Province]] |parent house = Kanasashi clan?
Ōmiwa clan? |titles = High priest (''Ōhōri'') of the [[Suwa-taisha|Upper Suwa Shrine]]
''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[Takashima Domain]]
|founder = [[Takeminakata]] (legendary)
Historically unknown |final ruler = |current head = |founding year = Unknown |dissolution = |ruled until = 1871 ([[:en:Abolition of the han system|''han'' system]] and [[State Shinto#Great Promulgation Campaign|hereditary priesthood]] abolished) |cadet branches = Suwa clan (諏方氏) (defunct)
Takatoo clan (高遠氏)
Hoshina clan (保科氏)
Chino clan (千野氏) }} The {{nihongo|'''Suwa clan'''|諏訪氏|Suwa-shi}}, also known as the '''Jin''' or '''Miwa clan''' (神氏, ''Miwa [[Uji (clan)|uji]] / Miwa-shi'' or ''Jinshi'') was a Japanese ''[[Shake (social class)|shake]]'' and [[samurai]] family. Originating from the area encompassing [[Lake Suwa]] in [[Shinano Province]] (modern-day [[Nagano Prefecture]]), it was originally a family of priests who served at the [[Suwa-taisha|Upper Shrine of Suwa]] located on the southwestern side of the lake.{{cite book|last1=Bocking|first1=Brian|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|date=2005|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1135797393|page=142|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6d-RAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA142}} By the [[Kamakura period]], it thrived as a prominent samurai clan with close ties to the [[Kamakura Shogunate|shogunate]]. Surviving the fall of both the Kamakura shogunate and the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] which it supported, its feud with local rival clans, and frequent clashes with its neighbor in [[Kai Province|Kai]], the [[Takeda clan]], during the [[Sengoku period]] (which ended in the extinction of the main family), by the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] the clan had split into two branches: one ruling the [[Suwa Domain]] of [[Shinano Province|Shinano]] as ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'', with the other continuing to serve as priests of Suwa Shrine until the [[Meiji (era)|Meiji period]]. ==Ancestry== === In legend === [[File:Suwa Daimyōjin - 諏訪大明神.jpg|left|thumb|Suwa Daimyōjin ([[Takeminakata]]) wearing hunting gear. Religious rites centered around hunting and agriculture were an integral part of Suwa Shrine's ritual calendar in the medieval period.]] Although the Suwa, which was the high priestly lineage of the Upper Shrine (上社 ''Kamisha'') of Suwa, one of the component shrines of [[Suwa-taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]], traditionally regarded themselves to be the descendants of the shrine's [[Kami|deity]], [[Takeminakata]] (also known as Suwa [[Myōjin|Daimyōjin]]),{{cite book|last1=Picken|first1=Stuart D.B.|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|date=28 December 2010|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0810871724|page=288|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&pg=PA288}} the clan's actual historical origins are shrouded in mystery. In the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Kujiki|Sendai Kuji Hongi]]'', Takeminakata is portrayed as a son of the god [[Ōkuninushi]] who fled to Suwa after his defeat at the hands of the god [[Takemikazuchi]], who was sent by the gods of [[Takamagahara|heaven]] to [[Kuni-yuzuri|claim the land]] held by his father in the name of the goddess [[Amaterasu]].{{cite book|last1=Chamberlain|first1=Basil|title=A translation of the "Ko-ji-ki" or Records of Ancient Matters|date=1882|url=http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj039.htm#fn_697}}{{cite book|author=J. Hackin|title=Asiatic Mythology: A Detailed Description and Explanation of the Mythologies of All the Great Nations of Asia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HAZrFhvqnTkC&pg=PA395|year=1932|publisher=Asian Educational Services|isbn=978-81-206-0920-4|page=395}}{{cite book|author=Jean Herbert|title=Shinto: At the Fountainhead of Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sg_JBQAAQBAJ&pg=PT437|date=18 October 2010|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90376-2|page=437}}{{cite book |author=Michael Ashkenazi|title=Handbook of Japanese Mythology|url=https://archive.org/details/handbookofjapane0000ashk|url-access=registration|date=1 January 2003 |publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-57607-467-1|pages=[https://archive.org/details/handbookofjapane0000ashk/page/267 267]–268}} Other myths (mostly of medieval provenance), however, portray the Suwa deity in a different light. In one story, Suwa Daimyōjin is an interloper who wrested control of Suwa from the indigenous god [[Moriya|Moriya]],{{cite book|author=Oh|first=Amana ChungHae|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hxulspIN_2UC&pg=PA157|title=Cosmogonical Worldview of Jomon Pottery|date=November 2011|publisher=Sankeisha|isbn=978-4-88361-924-5|page=157}} the mythical ancestor of the Moriya (守矢氏) clan, one of the priestly families of the Upper Shrine.Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya Jinchō-ke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). pp. 2–3.''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' (神長守矢氏系譜), in {{cite book|editor=Suwa Kyōikukai (諏訪教育会)|title=諏訪史料叢書 巻28 (Suwa shiryō-sōsho, vol. 28)|date=1931|location=Suwa|publisher=Suwa Kyōikukai|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1185913/24|language=ja}} In another myth, the god is said to have chosen an eight-year-old boy to become his priest (祝, ''hōri''; [[:en:Historical kana orthography|historical orthography]]: ''hafuri'') and [[Shintai|living incarnation]] by clothing the latter with his own garments. This boy is eventually said to have become the founding ancestor of the Suwa clan.Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=u2Mf7Ef60FkC&pg=PA11 諏訪史年表] (Suwa Shinenpyō).'' Nagano: Suwa Kyōikukai. p. 11.{{in lang|ja}}{{cite web|title=大祝有員 (Ōhōri Arikazu)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030504.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City |language=ja}}{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa Clan)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City |language=ja}}{{cite book|last1=Yamada|first1=Taka|title=Shinto Symbols|url=http://www.dl.ndl.go.jp/view/download/digidepo_9602313_po_CRJ-187.PDF?contentNo=1&alternativeNo=|page=8}}{{cite journal|last1=Ihara|first1=Kesao|title=鎌倉期の諏訪神社関係史料にみる神道と仏道 : 中世御記文の時代的特質について (Shinto and Buddhism as Depicted in Historical Materials Related to Suwa Shrines of the Kamakura Period : Temporal Characteristics of Medieval Imperial Writings)|journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History|date=2008-03-31|volume=139|pages=157–185|url=https://rekihaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=1538&item_no=1&page_id=13&block_id=41|language=ja}} Medieval tradition usually identified a semi-legendary individual named Arikazu (有員), who is said to have lived in the early [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] during the reigns of the emperors [[Emperor Kanmu|Kanmu]] (reigned 781-806), [[:en:Emperor Heizei|Heizei]] (806-809), and [[:en:Emperor Saga|Saga]] (809-823), to be this child.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=u2Mf7Ef60FkC|title=諏訪史年表 (Suwa shinenpyō)|date=1938|publisher=Suwa Kyōikukai|editor=Suwa Kyōikukai|location=Nagano|page=11}}Miyasaka (1987). p. 35.{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa Clan)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{in lang|ja}}}} The ''[[Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba]]'' (1356) for example relates:
At the beginning of the god's [[Honji suijaku|manifestation]], he took off his robe, put them on an eight year old boy, and dubbed him 'great priest' (''Ōhōri''). The god declared, "I do not have a body and so make this priest (''hōri'') my body." This [boy] is Arikazu (有員), the priest of the sacred robe (御衣祝 ''Misogihōri''), the founding ancestor of the Miwa (Jin) clan.
However, a brief text attached to a genealogical record of the Suwa clan discovered in the ''Ōhōri'''s residence in 1884Ihara (2008). p. 261. instead portrays Arikazu as a descendant of Kumako (神子 or 熊子), a son of a ''[[kuni no miyatsuko]]'' (provincial governor) of [[Shinano Province]], who is claimed to have founded the Upper Shrine during the reign of [[:en:Emperor Yōmei|Emperor Yōmei]] (585-587).''Ōhōri-bon Jinshi Keizu'' (大祝本 神氏系図), cited in {{cite book|last1=Kanai|first1=Tenbi|title=Suwa-shinkō-shi (諏訪信仰史)|date=1982|publisher=Meicho Shuppan|pages=107, 190}}
When Kumako was eight years old, the revered deity appeared, took off his robe and put them on Kumako. After declaring, "I do not have a body and so make you my body," he disappeared. This [Kumako] is the ancestor of Arikazu of the Miwa (Jin) clan, the ''Misogihōri''. In the second year of Emperor Yōmei, Kumako built a sanctuary at the foot of the mountain at the southern side of the lake.
Another genealogical record, that of the [[Aso clan]] ([[:ja:阿蘇氏|阿蘇氏]]) of [[Aso Shrine]] in [[Kyushu]] (discovered in 1956), similarly identifies Otoei (乙頴) - there given the alias 'Kumako' - as the "''Ōhōri'' of the great deity of Suwa" (諏訪大神大祝) and narrates the same legend as those found above.''Ihon Asoshi Keizu'' (異本阿蘇氏系図), cited in Kanai (1982). p. 109. Recent reappraisals of these two genealogies, however, have cast doubt on their authenticity and reliability as historical sources.Ihara (2008). pp. 260-262.{{cite web|author=Fukushima, Masaki (福島正樹)|title=信濃古代の通史叙述をめぐって (Shinano kodai no tsūshi jojutsu o megutte)|url=http://user1.matsumoto.ne.jp/~fukusima/yamakawa.htm|access-date=2017-09-24|website=科野太郎の古代・中世史の部屋}}{{cite journal|author1=Itō, Rintarō (伊藤麟太朗)|title=所謂『阿蘇氏系図』について (Iwayuru 'Aso-shi Keizu' ni tsuite)|journal=Shinano (信濃)|date=1994|volume=46|issue=8|pages=696–697|publisher=Shinano Shigakukai (信濃史学会)}}{{cite journal|author1=Murasaki, Machiko (村崎真智子)|title=異本阿蘇氏系図試論 (Ihon Aso-shi keizu shiron)|journal=Hito, mono, kotoba no jinruigaku: Kokubu Naoichi Hakushi beiju kinen ronbunshū (ヒト・モノ・コトバの人類学. 国分直一博士米寿記念論文集)|date=1996|pages=202–218|publisher=Keiyūsha (慶友社)}}{{cite book|author1=Asoshina, Yasuo (阿蘇品 保夫)|title=阿蘇社と大宮司―中世の阿蘇 (Aso-sha to Daiguji: chusei no Aso)|date=1999|publisher=Ichinomiya-machi (一の宮町)|isbn=978-4877550462}}For a contrary viewpoint, cf. {{cite web|author1=Hōga, Yoshio (宝賀寿男)|title=村崎真智子氏論考「異本阿蘇氏系図試論」等を読む|url=http://wwr2.ucom.ne.jp/hetoyc15/|date=2006}} Apart from these candidates, the clan has also been claimed to descend from the [[Seiwa Genji]] via Minamoto no Mitsuyasu (one of the sons of [[Minamoto no Tsunemoto]]).{{cite web|title=諏訪氏 (Suwa-shi)|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/suwa_k.html|website=播磨屋 (harimaya.com)|language=ja}}{{cite book|last1=Papinot|first1=Edmond|title=Historical and Geographical Dictionary of Japan, Volume 2|date=1910|page=[https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete/page/n148 611]|url=https://archive.org/details/PapinotDictionaryOfJapanVolume2Complete}} ==The Suwa ''Ōhōri''== [[File:Suwa taisha Kamisha Maemiya , 諏訪大社 上社 前宮 - panoramio (13).jpg|thumb|''Kamisha Maemiya'', one of the two main shrines that comprise the Upper Shrine of Suwa. The Upper Shrine's high priest or ''Ōhōri'' resided in this area during the medieval period.]] In antiquity, the Suwa clan produced the Upper Shrine (上社 ''Kamisha'') of Suwa's high priest known as the ''Ōhōri'' (大祝 'great priest', [[:en:Historical kana orthography|old orthography]]: おほはふり ''Ohohafuri''; also rendered as ''Ōhafuri''), who was worshiped as [[Arahitogami|the living avatar]] of the shrine's deity during his period in office.{{cite book|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|year=1988|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}} The ''Ōhōri'', who traditionally assumed the position at a young age (ideally between the ages of eight to fifteen), was assisted [[Suwa taisha#Priests|by five priests]] headed by the ''Jinchōkan'' (神長官) of the Moriya clan, who oversaw the Upper Shrine's religious rituals, many of which are centered around the worship of [[List of agricultural gods|agricultural]] and [[List of fertility deities|fertility god(s)]] called [[Mishaguji]]. The ''Jinchōkan'' was believed to have the prerogative to [[Spirit possession|summon the Mishaguji onto individuals and objects]] whenever its presence was called for.Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya-jinchō-ke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 4. {{in lang|ja}}Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In {{cite book|author1=Ueda|author2=Gorai|author3=Ōbayashi|author4=Miyasaka, M.|author5=Miyasaka, Y.|title=御柱祭と諏訪大社 (Onbashira-sai to Suwa-taisha)|location=Nagano|publisher=Chikuma Shobō|isbn=978-4480841810|pages=25–26|language=ja}} Though officially the Upper Shrine's chief priest and as incarnate deity, an object of worship, the Suwa ''Ōhōri'' had little, if any, actual power over the shrine's affairs, which rested in the hands of the Moriya ''Jinchōkan'', with his unique relationship to the Mishaguji and his knowledge of closely guarded secret traditions passed down via word of mouth only to the heir to the office.Moriya (1991), p. 5. In fact, it was due to the ''Jinchōkan'' summoning the Mishaguji onto the ''Ōhōri'' during the investiture ceremony that the latter became a living deity.{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)|language=ja}}Miyasaka (1987). p. 29. ===Investiture ceremony=== The full rite of investiture into the office of ''Ōhōri'' as practiced in the late medieval period involved the candidate first undergoing a twenty-two day period of strict [[ritual purification]] in the ''Maemiya'' (前宮 'old shrine'), one of the Upper Shrine's two component shrines. During the day of the ceremony itself, the ''Jinchōkan'' led the candidate by the hand before a sacred tree west of the ''Gōdono'' (神殿), the ''Ōhōri'''s residence during his term located west of the ''Maemiya'', under which was a flat rock known as the ''kanameishi'' (要石 'keystone'). During the ceremony, this rock is surrounded a makeshift enclosure or hut and a mat of reeds was placed over it for the boy to sit on.Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 722. Inside this enclosure, the ''Jinchōkan'' dressed the boy in full ritual attire: traditional makeup (''[[oshiroi]]'', ''[[ohaguro]]'', ''[[Rouge (cosmetics)|beni]]'' and ''[[:en:Hikimayu|mayuzumi]]''), a dull yellow-green ''[[sokutai]]'', a ''[[:en:Hakama|Hakama]]'', and a crown (''kanmuri'').Fujimori, Akira (1991). ''Ōhōri sokui no keshō-dōgu'' (大祝即位の化粧道具). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 37. {{in lang|ja}} The ''Jinchōkan'' then summoned the Mishaguji (who as a [[nature spirit]] was believed to manifest on rocks and trees) to the ''kanameishi'' via secret [[Mantra|incantations]]. Via the rock, the Mishaguji was then believed to enter the child's body, thereby turning him into a [[Arahitogami|living god]].Miyasaka (1992). p. 53.Miyasaka (1987). p. 28-29. [[File:Suwa taisha Kamisha Maemiya , 諏訪大社 上社 前宮 内御玉殿 - panoramio (2).jpg|thumb|left|The Uchi-no-mitama-den (内御玉殿)]] After being consecrated, the ''Ōhōri'' visited the various shrines of the Upper Shrine complex. In another shrine in the ''Maemiya'' area, the Uchi-no-mitama-den (内御霊殿), wherein was kept the sacred treasures of the Upper Shrine (a bell, a [[:en:Bronze mirror|mirror]], a [[:en:Bit (horse)|bit]] and a [[saddle]]) that were supposedly brought to the region by Suwa Daimyōjin himself,{{cite book|editor=Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai|title=諏訪市史 上巻 原始・古代・中世 (Suwa Shishi, vol. 1)|date=1995|location=Suwa|page=718|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/9572217}} the ''Ōhōri'' made a ritual declaration (申立 ''mōshitate'') that he has become the god's new 'body' and will henceforth avoid [[Kegare|impurity]].Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 696, 722-723. As time went on the ritual became increasingly simplified and later, was supposedly even omitted altogether, with the ''ōhōri'' simply assuming the position without any ceremony.{{cite web|title=大祝即位式場|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/zatugaku/sokui.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}} ===Role=== During his term, the incumbent ''Ōhōri'' was treated as the physical manifestation of Suwa Daimyōjin. In 1186, [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] officially recognized the ''Ōhōri'' as the god's incarnation in a letter to his subordinates, declaring that the ''Ōhōri'''s orders are those of the god himself.Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 696. The ''Ōhōri'' was expected to live a life of ritual purity and was also forbidden to step outside the boundaries of Suwa region under pain of divine punishment.{{cite web|title=諏訪大明神 (Suwa-daimyōjin)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E5%A4%A7%E6%98%8E%E7%A5%9E.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)|language=ja}}Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 695. During his term of office, the ''Ōhōri'' originally resided in a building near the Suwa ''Maemiya'' known as the ''Gōdono'' (神殿). Reflecting its being the residence of an incarnate deity, the ''Maemiya'' area and its vicinity was known during the Middle Ages as the ''Gōbara'' (神原), the 'god's field'.{{cite book|editor1-last=Tanigawa|editor1-first=Kenichi|title=Nihon no kamigami: Jinja to seichi, vol. 9: Mino, Hida, Shinano (日本の神々―神社と聖地〈9〉美濃・飛騨・信濃)|date=1987|publisher=Hakusuisha|isbn=978-4560025093|pages=138–139}} Should an incumbent ''Ōhōri'' die while in office, his corpse was immediately brought before the Uchi-no-mitama-den where he was ceremonially retired - the idea being that the ''Ōhōri'''s spirit was temporarily deposited in the shrine until a new candidate was chosen.Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). pp. 718-719. Originally, the deceased priest was buried wearing hunting attire (such as that supposedly worn by Suwa Daimyōjin) and with hair and beard kept unshaven.Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. pp. 719. However, in 1465, with the death of then ''Ōhōri'' Yorinaga (頼長), the local priesthood began to adopt the Buddhist custom of [[:en:Cremation|Cremation]]. By the early 17th century, the ''Ōhōri'''s residence was moved from the ''Maemiya'' to [https://www.google.co.jp/maps/place/%E3%80%92392-0015+Nagano-ken,+Suwa-shi,+Nakasu,+%E5%A4%A7%E7%A5%9D%E5%B1%8B%E6%95%B7/@36.000373,138.1261382,18z/data=!4m5!3m4!1s0x601c56f08ec073dd:0x2f127865a478c42a!8m2!3d36.0003473!4d138.1271388 a place] in what is now Nakasu, [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa City]]. ==History== ===From the Heian period to the Sengoku period=== In the meantime, other male members of the clan aside from the ''ōhōri'' - who cannot step outside the boundaries of the region, as well as come into contact with sources of impurity such as the flesh and blood of men or horses - began to pursue military careers. One of the first recorded warriors from the clan was Tamenaka (為仲), a son of then ''ōhōri'' Tamenobu (為信). Tamenaka served under [[Minamoto no Yoshiie]] during the [[Zenkunen War]] (1051-1063) under the orders of his father, who could not participate himself due to his priestly status. He then also served again under Yoshiie in the later [[:en:Gosannen War|Gosannen War]] of the 1080s, this time despite opposition from his family due to him already inheriting the position of ''ōhōri'' from Tamenobu in the interim between the two wars. Tamenaka's eventual suicide out of shame after his subordinates had a violent quarrel with [[Minamoto no Yoshimitsu]]'s men during a feast held by the latter was considered to be divine punishment for his violation of the ban.Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). pp. 23-24.{{cite web|title=源氏御家人としての諏訪氏|url=http://rarememory.justhpbs.jp/kama/na.htm#%E5%BE%8C%E4%B8%89%E5%B9%B4%E3%81%AE%E5%BD%B9%E3%81%AE%E8%AB%8F%E8%A8%AA%E7%82%BA%E4%BB%B2%E3%81%AE%E5%8E%BB%E5%B0%B1|website=信州歴史散歩}}{{cite book|last1=Miyachi|first1=Naokazu|title=諏訪史 第二卷 前編 (Suwa-shi, vol. 2, part 1)|date=1931|publisher=Shinano kyōikukai Suwa-bukai|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4hBVjsO2GOgC|pages=274–275|language=ja}} Due to the circumstances of his father's death, Tamenaka's son, Tamemori (為盛) did not inherit the office of ''ōhōri'', it instead passing in succession to Tamenaka's three younger brothers, two of whom died within mere days of their investiture. It would be the youngest brother, Tamesada (為貞), who would turn out to successfully pass down the priesthood to his progeny. By the [[Kamakura period]], the clan - now renowned as being both a priestly and a warrior clan - rose to national prominence as vassals (''[[:en:Gokenin|Gokenin]]'') of the [[Kamakura shogunate|shogunate]] and later, flourished greatly under the patronage of the [[Hōjō clan]]. The clan's fortunes waned with the fall of the Kamakura shogunate and the defeat of the [[Southern Court|Southern Imperial Court]] (which the clan supported) during the [[Nanboku-chō period]]. During the [[Muromachi period]], the Suwa were involved both in a feud with the Kanasashi clan of the ''Shimosha'' which supported the [[Northern Court]], and interclan strife between the head family (惣領家 ''sōryō-ke'') and the ''ōhōri-ke'' (大祝家), a branch of the clan that had come to assume the priestly duties. With the defeat of the Kanasashi and the head family's reattainment of the position of ''ōhori'', the clan became a [[:en:Daimyō|regional power]], clashing with the [[Takeda clan]] - originally their allies - during the [[Sengoku period]]. The clan again suffered a setback with [[Suwa Yorishige (daimyo)|Suwa Yorishige]]'s defeat in the hands of [[Takeda Shingen]] (who was, ironically, a staunch devotee of Suwa-myōjin) in 1542 and with his suicide in 1544, the extinction of the main family; his cousin Yoritada (諏訪頼忠, 1536-1606), who succeeded Yorishige's younger brother Yoritaka (諏訪頼高, 1528-1542) as ''ōhōri'', was spared. After the Takeda was destroyed by an alliance of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]], Yoritada allied himself with the latter, who eventually reinstated Yoritada in his family domain in 1601. ===Edo period onwards=== [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the Moriya clan's estate grounds in [[:en:Chino, Nagano|Chino City]], Nagano.]]Yoritada's eldest son, Yorimizu (頼水, 1571-1641) became the first ''daimyō'' to rule [[Suwa Domain]], with the office of ''ōhōri'' passing down to his fourth son, Yorihiro (頼広). With this, the clan effectively split into two branches: the ''daimyō'' line and the ''ōhōri'' line. To distinguish themselves from the ''daimyō'' line, the priestly line altered one of the [[:en:Chinese characters|Chinese characters]] of their surname (from 諏'''訪''' to 諏'''方'''). All in all, ten generations served as ''daimyō'' of Suwa Domain until the abolition of the [[:en:Han system|Han system]] during the [[Meiji period]].{{cite web|title=高島藩 (Takashima-han)|url=http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~me4k-skri/han/hokuriku/takasima.html|website=Edo 300 Han HTML|language=ja}} Meanwhile, the establishment of [[State Shinto]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priesthood, including that of Suwa Grand Shrine. Local clans such as the Suwa lost control of the shrine's traditional priestly offices (which in turn became defunct) as government appointees began to manage the shrine, which passed under state control. The last Suwa ''ōhōri'', the fifteenth since Yorihiro, died in 2002 with no heirs.{{cite web|script-title=ja:最後の大祝|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/saigo.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人|language=ja}} ==See also== *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Moriya|Moreya]] *[[Suwa Domain]] *[[Suwa-taisha|Suwa Taisha]] *[[Suwa Province]] *[[Takeda Shingen]] *[[Takeminakata]] ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} {{Suwa Faith}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Pages without meta categories]] [[sn:Suwa clan]][[sn:Suwa clan]][[Category:japanese clans]] }} [[sn:Suwa clan]] [[en:Suwa clan]] [[Category:Pages without translation templates]] [[Category:Pages with valid en interwikis]] [[Category:pages with valid en interwikis 2]] [[de:Suwa (Klan)]] [[fa:خاندان سووا]] [[fr:Clan Suwa]] [[id:Klan Suwa]] [[it:Clan Suwa]] [[ja:諏訪氏]] [[ko:스와씨]] [[pt:Clã Suwa]] [[ru:Сува (род)]]
